cases.audioScript: On Australia Day, January twenty-sixth, 1966, three children from Adelaide set off for Glenelg beach, a short bus ride from home. Jane Beaumont was nine. Her sister Arnna was seven, and their brother Grant was four. They never came home. Police found witnesses who had seen the children near the beach with a tall, thin-faced, sun-tanned man in his mid-thirties. They were confirmed at Colley Reserve and at a cake shop in Glenelg. After that, they vanished. Police believe the children were abducted and murdered. Their remains have never been found. Over the decades, detectives have followed thousands of leads. In 2013 and again in 2018, police dug at a factory site in North Plympton after new tips. Nothing of interest was found. A privately organized dig in 2025 also found no remains. The South Australian government offers a one-million-dollar reward for information leading to a conviction, or to finding the children. Nearly sixty years later, the Beaumont children remain one of Australia's most enduring mysteries.
cases.summary: On Australia Day, Jan. 26, 1966, Jane (9), Arnna (7) and Grant (4) Beaumont took a short bus trip from their home in Somerton Park to Glenelg beach in Adelaide and failed to return (National Missing Persons Coordination Centre). Witnesses saw the children near the beach with a tall, thin-faced, sun-tanned man in his mid-30s; confirmed sightings were at Colley Reserve and a cake shop in Moseley Street, Glenelg. Police suspect the children were abducted and murdered (NMPCC). In 2014 the South Australian government raised the reward to A$1 million, payable for information leading to a conviction or the recovery of remains (Sydney Morning Herald; Guardian/AAP). SA Police excavated part of the New Castalloy factory site in North Plympton in 2013 and again in February 2018 after Channel Seven supplied geophysical results; the 2018 dig found only animal bones and was called off (Guardian/AAP; ABC). A seven-day dig at the site organized by independent MP Frank Pangallo ended on March 1, 2025, without finding remains; SA Police said the theory behind it was not supported by evidence (ABC).
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. Remains never found.

cases.audioScript: On July twenty-ninth, 2023, Erin Patterson hosted a lunch at her home in Leongatha, a small town in South Gippsland, Victoria. Her guests were her former parents-in-law, Don and Gail Patterson, both seventy, Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, sixty-six, and Heather's husband, Ian, a church pastor. She served beef Wellington. Within days, Don, Gail and Heather were dead. Ian spent nearly two months in hospital with critical organ damage before he recovered. The dish contained death cap mushrooms. In July 2025, after a trial in the Supreme Court of Victoria, a jury found Erin Patterson guilty of three counts of murder and one count of attempted murder. In September 2025, Justice Christopher Beale sentenced her to life in prison with a non-parole period of thirty-three years. She appealed. On October thirtieth, 2026, Victoria's Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal and went further, resentencing her to life without parole. Her only remaining avenue is an application to the High Court of Australia. Today the case is remembered for Don, Gail and Heather, three people who were loved in their community.
cases.summary: On July 29, 2023, Erin Patterson served a beef Wellington lunch at her Leongatha home to her former parents-in-law Don and Gail Patterson, both 70, Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, 66, and Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson. The meal contained death cap mushrooms. Don, Gail and Heather died; Ian spent nearly two months in hospital and recovered (SBS). Patterson was tried in the Supreme Court of Victoria and on July 7, 2025 a jury found her guilty of three counts of murder and one count of attempted murder. On Sept. 8, 2025 Justice Christopher Beale sentenced her to life imprisonment with a 33-year non-parole period (ABC; AustLII sentence R v Patterson [2025] VSC 557). On Oct. 30, 2026 the Victorian Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal against conviction and upheld a prosecution appeal, setting aside the non-parole period and resentencing her to life without parole (SBS, ABC). ABC reported her remaining avenue is a High Court of Australia special-leave application. Separate attempted-murder charges concerning her estranged husband were dropped before trial and are not part of the convictions.
cases.solvedHow: Solved by police investigation and jury trial; convictions upheld on appeal (2026).

cases.audioScript: On the afternoon of Saturday, February second, 2008, twenty-four-year-old real estate agent Lindsay Buziak went to show a home in Saanich, British Columbia. The house sat on a quiet cul-de-sac in the Gordon Head neighbourhood. She arrived for a five-thirty showing with a couple who said they were buyers. Police say Lindsay was stabbed to death in an upstairs bedroom. Investigators later said the couple had arranged the meeting with a cellphone registered under a fake name in Metro Vancouver. They have never been identified, and no one has ever been arrested. In 2021, Saanich police formed a new task force. Working with the FBI and the RCMP, they began retesting evidence with DNA technology that did not exist in 2008. In late 2025, Lindsay's mother said she had heard the investigation was ending. Police answered that the case remains active and ongoing. Every February second, her father leads a Walk for Justice from Saanich Municipal Hall to the B.C. Legislature. He is still asking for someone to come forward.
cases.summary: Lindsay Buziak, a 24-year-old real estate agent, was stabbed to death on Feb. 2, 2008, while showing an empty home on a cul-de-sac (De Sousa Place) in Saanich's Gordon Head neighbourhood (CBC; Saanich News). Police said she was lured by an unidentified couple posing as prospective buyers to a 5:30 p.m. showing; the meeting was arranged with a cellphone later found to be registered to a fake name in Metro Vancouver. She was killed in an upstairs bedroom (CBC). No arrests have been made. On Jan. 31, 2021, Saanich Police (file 08-2682) announced a task force of new investigators, assisted by the FBI and RCMP, and said retesting of evidence, including DNA and digital evidence, had produced new leads (Saanich PD; CBC). In November 2025, after her mother posted a video saying the active investigation had ended, Saanich Police said the investigation "remains active and ongoing" (Saanich News). Her father leads an annual Walk for Justice each Feb. 2 (Saanich News). Tips: Saanich Police, 250-475-4321 (Saanich News, Nov. 2025; CHEK News).

cases.audioScript: Through the late 1990s and into 2001, women kept disappearing from Vancouver's Downtown Eastside. Many were poor, many struggled with addiction, and many were Indigenous. For years, their families said no one was listening. In February 2002, police searched a pig farm in nearby Port Coquitlam owned by Robert William Pickton. What they found turned it into the largest crime scene in Canadian history. Pickton was charged with murdering twenty-six women. In December 2007, a jury in New Westminster found him guilty of second-degree murder in the deaths of six: Sereena Abotsway, Mona Wilson, Andrea Joesbury, Brenda Wolfe, Georgina Papin and Marnie Frey. He was sentenced to life in prison, with no chance of parole for twenty-five years. In 2010, the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the convictions, and prosecutors decided not to try him on the other twenty charges. A provincial inquiry later found blatant failures by police. In May 2024, Pickton was attacked in a Quebec prison and died. Many families of the missing women are still waiting for answers.
cases.summary: Robert William Pickton, a pig farmer from Port Coquitlam, B.C., was arrested in 2002 after the Project Evenhanded task force (Vancouver Police and RCMP) searched his farm beginning Feb. 5, 2002 (Canadian Encyclopedia; CBC). He was eventually charged with 26 counts of murder of women from Vancouver's Downtown Eastside (Canadian Encyclopedia; CBC). On Dec. 9, 2007, a B.C. Supreme Court jury in New Westminster found him not guilty of first-degree murder but guilty of second-degree murder in the deaths of Sereena Abotsway, Mona Wilson, Andrea Joesbury, Brenda Wolfe, Georgina Papin and Marnie Frey (CBC; Globe and Mail; Guardian). On Dec. 11, 2007, he was sentenced to life with no parole eligibility for 25 years, the maximum (CBC). The Supreme Court of Canada dismissed his appeal and affirmed the convictions on July 30, 2010 (SCC docket 33288; CBC). Prosecutors announced on Aug. 4, 2010 that they would not proceed on the 20 remaining charges (Canadian Encyclopedia). The Missing Women Commission of Inquiry's 2012 report found "blatant failures" by police (Canadian Encyclopedia; CBC). Pickton was assaulted at Port-Cartier Institution in Quebec on May 19, 2024, and died May 31, 2024 (CBC).
cases.solvedHow: A tip about illegal firearms gave police grounds for a search warrant at the farm; evidence found there led to murder charges. Convicted at trial in 2007.

cases.audioScript: On June twelfth, 1999, fifteen-year-old Sharmini Anandavel left her family's Toronto apartment. She told her parents she was going out to see about a new job. She never came home. Days later, police found a phony employment application in her room, and came to believe that whoever killed her had used the promise of a job to lure her away. Four months later, on October twelfth, her skeletal remains were found in a shallow grave in a wooded ravine beside the Don River, in a park in northeast Toronto. Toronto police have said they had a suspect in mind and questioned that person several times, but did not have enough evidence to lay a charge. Her parents, who had come to Canada in 1993, stood beside detectives and begged for anyone with information to come forward. More than twenty-five years later, no one has been charged in Sharmini's murder. If you know anything about what happened to Sharmini Anandavel in the summer of 1999, contact the Toronto Police Service Homicide Squad, or Crime Stoppers at one eight hundred, two two two, tips.

cases.audioScript: In August 2007, twenty-year-old Christina Calayca of Toronto was on a camping trip with friends at Rainbow Falls Provincial Park, along Highway Seventeen near Schreiber, Ontario, on the north shore of Lake Superior. At about six thirty on the morning of August sixth, she told a companion she was going for a jog. She was last seen on a roadway in the park's campground. She never came back. The Ontario Provincial Police launched a huge search, on the ground, from the air, on the water, and with specialist teams trained in high-angle rope rescue on the steep, rugged terrain west of the park. They found no trace of her. Police say it is not known whether her disappearance involved foul play, but it cannot be ruled out. In 2023, the OPP renewed its appeal, asking anyone in the area to report bones or clothing matching what she wore: a blue hoodie, a maroon and purple striped shirt, black pants and white running shoes. If you have any information about Christina Calayca, contact the Ontario Provincial Police, or Crime Stoppers.

The OPP conducted extensive ground, air, marine and specialist searches; a planned continuation by the Provincial Emergency Response Team, with high-angle rope searches west of the park, was cancelled for weather in November 2007. In 2023 the OPP renewed its appeal, saying foul play could not be ruled out and asking people to report any remains or clothing matching what she wore. She has never been found. Tips: OPP, 1-888-310-1122, or Crime Stoppers, 1-800-222-TIPS (8477) (Toronto Sun, 2023). Canada's Missing lists the Nipigon OPP file as TP07020640.

cases.audioScript: On the evening of May sixth, 2013, Tim Bosma, a thirty-two-year-old husband and father from Ancaster, Ontario, took two men on a test drive of the pickup truck he was selling online. He never came home. His burned remains were found days later. The two men were Dellen Millard and his friend Mark Smich. In 2016, a jury in Hamilton found them both guilty of first-degree murder. Prosecutors said the pair planned to steal the truck and kill its owner, and that Bosma's body was burned in an animal incinerator Millard had bought. Investigators then looked back. Laura Babcock, a twenty-three-year-old Toronto woman who had been involved with Millard, had vanished in July 2012. In 2017, Millard and Smich were convicted of her murder too. Her remains have never been found. And in November 2012, Millard's father, Wayne, had been found shot in his Toronto home. Police first deemed it a suicide. In 2018, a judge found Dellen Millard guilty of murdering him. Three victims, three trials, three first-degree murder convictions. Ontario's top court later upheld the conviction for his father's murder.
cases.summary: Laura Babcock, 23, vanished from Toronto in July 2012. On Nov. 29, 2012, Wayne Millard, 71, a wealthy aviation executive, was shot in the eye while he slept in his Etobicoke home; police first deemed his death a suicide (CBC; Globe and Mail). On May 6, 2013, Tim Bosma, 32, of Ancaster, disappeared after taking Dellen Millard and Mark Smich on a test drive of a pickup truck he had listed for sale online; his burned remains were found days later (CityNews; Globe and Mail). The Crown said the pair planned to steal the truck and kill its owner, and that Bosma's body was burned in an animal incinerator Millard had bought (CityNews; CBC). On June 17, 2016, an Ontario Superior Court jury in Hamilton found Millard and Smich guilty of first-degree murder in Bosma's death; both received life sentences (CBC; National Post). In 2017 a Toronto jury convicted both of first-degree murder of Babcock, whose body was burned in an animal incinerator and never found; the judge ordered their life sentences served consecutively to the Bosma sentences (CBC). In September 2018, Justice Maureen Forestell found Dellen Millard guilty of first-degree murder of his father, finding he bought the gun used and set up a false alibi (Globe and Mail; CBC). The Ontario Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal of that conviction, calling the evidence "overwhelming" (CBC, April 2023).

cases.audioScript: In March 1998, twenty-three-year-old Amy Lynn Bradley of Virginia was on a Caribbean cruise with her family aboard Royal Caribbean's Rhapsody of the Seas. On March twenty-third, the ship left Aruba, headed for Curaçao. In the early morning hours of Tuesday, March twenty-fourth, as the ship sailed toward port, Amy went missing. According to the Charley Project, she and her brother had sat on their cabin balcony until about five-thirty that morning, and two passengers later reported seeing her on an elevator to the top deck. She has never been found. The FBI still lists Amy among its missing persons and is offering a reward of up to one hundred thousand dollars for information leading to her recovery, or to the identification, arrest and conviction of anyone responsible. Amy was born in Petersburg, Virginia. She played basketball in college and loved her family. Over the years there have been reported sightings, but none has led to her. If you were on that cruise, or you have seen anyone you believe could be Amy, the FBI asks you to submit a tip at tips dot F B I dot gov.
cases.summary: Amy Lynn Bradley, 23, of Chesterfield County, Virginia, was traveling with her family on Royal Caribbean's Rhapsody of the Seas in March 1998. The FBI says the ship departed Aruba on Monday, March 23, 1998, bound for Curaçao, and that Bradley went missing in the early morning hours of Tuesday, March 24. The ship then called at Curaçao, St. Maarten and St. Thomas before returning to San Juan on March 28. The Charley Project, citing case records, says she and her brother sat on their suite's balcony until about 5:30 a.m. and that two passengers saw her riding an elevator toward the top deck around 6 a.m.; those sequence details come from a database summary and are stamped accordingly. The FBI lists the case under Kidnappings and Missing Persons and offers a reward of up to $100,000. Reported sightings over the years have not been confirmed. Netflix's three-part docuseries Amy Bradley Is Missing premiered July 16, 2025. No one has been charged. The case is filed under Curaçao because the disappearance occurred on the approach to Willemstad; her Virginia home county is a secondary location.

cases.audioScript: Just after midnight on June twenty-sixth, 2014, Anchorage police got a 911 call from a home on the city's Hillside. The caller said twenty-year-old Breanna Moore, known as Bree, had just been shot. Officers found Bree dead of a single gunshot wound to the head. Her boyfriend, twenty-two-year-old Joshua Almeda, was taken in for questioning. Police arrested him that same day and charged him with second-degree murder. Almeda told police he had found the gun with her body. But in 2015, he pleaded guilty to second-degree murder. In April 2016, an Anchorage judge sentenced him to seventy-five years in prison, saying the killing was closer to a deliberate shooting than a reckless one. Bree's family turned their grief into action. Her parents pushed for a state law on teen dating violence. In 2018, Alaska's governor signed a bill renaming the state's school program the Bree Moore Teen Dating Violence Awareness and Prevention Program. Bree was a curly-haired young woman with her whole life ahead of her. Today her name is used to teach Alaska's teenagers the warning signs.
cases.summary: At about 12:30 a.m. on June 26, 2014, Anchorage police received a 911 call from a home in the 10600 block of Treeline Court reporting that Breanna Richelle Moore, 20, had been shot. Officers found her dead of a single gunshot wound to the head (APD). Her boyfriend, Joshua Almeda, 22, was questioned and that day arrested and charged with second-degree murder and weapons offenses. The Anchorage Daily News reported he told police he had found the gun with her body. Almeda pleaded guilty to second-degree murder in 2015. On April 19, 2016, Anchorage Superior Court Judge Philip Volland sentenced him to 75 years, within a 10-to-99-year range, saying the killing was closer to a deliberate shooting than a reckless one and citing his criminal history (ADN). Her parents campaigned for dating-violence education; in July 2018 Gov. Bill Walker signed HB 214, renaming the school program the Bree Moore Teen Dating Violence Awareness and Prevention Program and funding training (KTUU).

cases.audioScript: On the morning of April tenth, 2001, a ranch house in Scottsdale, Arizona, exploded and caught fire. When firefighters dug through the debris, they found Mary Fisher and her two children, twelve-year-old Brittney and ten-year-old Bobby. Police say all three had been killed before the fire, and that a gas line to the house had been severed and rigged to explode. The husband and father, Robert Fisher, was gone, and so was the family dog, Blue. The evening before, surveillance video showed him withdrawing two hundred eighty dollars from an ATM, the last confirmed sighting. Ten days later, on April twentieth, investigators found the family's Toyota 4Runner in the woods near Payson, in the Tonto National Forest. Blue was waiting under the vehicle. Robert Fisher was not. He is charged with three counts of first-degree murder and arson, and the FBI still lists him as wanted. He has never been found, and he has never been tried. Scottsdale detectives say they still follow every tip. If you have information, contact the FBI at tips dot f b i dot gov, or Scottsdale police.

cases.audioScript: In March 1963, an eighteen-year-old movie theater worker in Phoenix, Arizona, was grabbed on her way home from work, forced into a car, driven into the desert and raped. Her description of the car led police to a twenty-three-year-old man named Ernesto Miranda. On March thirteenth, officers arrested him and questioned him for about two hours. He signed a written confession, and a jury convicted him of kidnapping and rape. But no one had told Miranda he had the right to stay silent or to have a lawyer. His appeal reached the United States Supreme Court, and on June thirteenth, 1966, in a five-to-four decision, the Court threw out his conviction. Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote that police must warn suspects of their rights before questioning them in custody. That is why officers today read the Miranda warning: you have the right to remain silent. Arizona retried Miranda in 1967 without the confession, using other evidence, and he was convicted again. He was later paroled, and in 1976 he was stabbed to death in a Phoenix bar fight. The woman he attacked has never been publicly named here, and her privacy is respected.
cases.summary: In the early hours of March 3, 1963, an 18-year-old Phoenix movie-theater worker was accosted on her way home, forced into a car, driven to the desert and raped (Encyclopedia.com account). Police traced a car to Ernesto Miranda, 23, who was arrested at his home on March 13, 1963, identified by the complaining witness, and interrogated for two hours, producing a signed written confession that was admitted at his trial; he was convicted of kidnapping and rape. On June 13, 1966, the U.S. Supreme Court (Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436, 5-4, opinion by Chief Justice Warren) reversed, holding that statements from custodial interrogation are inadmissible unless the suspect is first warned of the right to remain silent and to counsel. Arizona retried Miranda in 1967 without the confession; testimony from his former partner about his admissions led to another conviction and a 20-to-30-year sentence. He was paroled and was stabbed to death in a Phoenix bar fight on Jan. 31, 1976.
cases.solvedHow: Solved by police tracing a car described by the victim, a lineup identification and a confession; after the Supreme Court excluded the confession, the 1967 retrial convicted him on other evidence.

cases.audioScript: On June twenty-fifth, 1995, the body of a woman was found in an off-roading area of Standard Wash, near Lake Havasu City, Arizona. She had been shot to death. At first she was a Jane Doe, but investigators later identified her as forty-eight-year-old Jean Andrae Brady. Detectives interviewed several people, including her ex-husband, but no suspect was ever identified. More than thirty years later, in September 2026, the Mohave County Sheriff's Office asked for new leads. They want to hear from anyone who knew Jean, or her associates in Lake Havasu City in 1995, or anyone who knows who might have had cause to harm her. Detectives also hope to find her relatives, so they can return boxes of personal belongings recovered from a storage unit she rented. Her parents died decades ago, and investigators believe her extended family may live in Missouri or Kansas. If you can help, call the Mohave County Sheriff's Office Special Investigations Unit at 928-753-0753, extension 4408.

cases.audioScript: In June 2008, thirty-year-old Travis Alexander was found dead in the shower of his home here in Mesa, Arizona. He had been stabbed many times and shot. At trial she claimed self-defense, saying Travis attacked her. Prosecutors said she killed him in a jealous rage. She was arrested and charged with first-degree murder, and the case went to trial in Phoenix. The televised trial in Phoenix drew a national audience, and on May eighth, 2013, a jury found her guilty of first-degree murder. But that jury could not agree on death or life, and in 2015 a second jury deadlocked too, with a single holdout. So the decision went to the judge. On April thirteenth, 2015, Judge Sherry Stephens sentenced Arias to natural life in prison, with no chance of parole, calling the crime especially cruel and noting she destroyed evidence and went to great lengths to hide her involvement. Travis's sisters told the court how hard it is to remember him alive.
cases.summary: Travis Alexander, 30, was found dead in the shower of his Mesa, Arizona, home in June 2008; he had been shot in the head and his throat was slashed. His former girlfriend Jodi Arias admitted stabbing and shooting him but claimed self-defense; prosecutors said she killed him in a jealous rage. A Maricopa County jury found Arias guilty of first-degree murder on May 8, 2013, but deadlocked on the penalty, and a second penalty jury deadlocked in March 2015 with one holdout against death. On April 13, 2015, Judge Sherry Stephens sentenced Arias to natural life without parole, saying the crime involved substantial planning, that Arias did not render aid, destroyed evidence and went to great lengths to conceal her involvement.

cases.audioScript: On Valentine's Day 2007, thirty-nine-year-old Jodine Serrin was at home in her condominium in Carlsbad, California. Jodine lived on her own and was active in local support groups, including the National Alliance for the Mentally Ill. That night, her parents could not reach her by phone, so around ten o'clock they let themselves in. A man was in their daughter's bedroom. Her father told him to get out, and the man fled. Jodine had been beaten, raped and strangled. She died of blunt force head injuries. For ten years the case stayed open. In 2017, investigators released a DNA-based composite from Parabon NanoLabs and announced a reward of fifty-two thousand dollars. Then DNA matching through the suspect's relatives pointed to a transient named David Mabrito. Oceanside police had kept an unprocessed DNA sample from a traffic stop, and it matched the crime scene evidence. Mabrito had died by suicide in 2011, so he was never charged. In November 2018, Carlsbad police said they had identified the person responsible. The chief said they never forgot Jodine.
cases.summary: Jodine Elizabeth Serrin, 39, was found murdered in her ground-level condominium in the 1900 block of Swallow Lane, Carlsbad, on Feb. 14, 2007. Her parents, unable to reach her by phone, let themselves in around 10 p.m.; her father encountered a man in the bedroom and told him to leave, then discovered she had been beaten, raped and strangled (NBC News; Times of San Diego). An autopsy found she died of blunt-force head injuries (Times of San Diego). On the 10th anniversary in 2017, Carlsbad police and the San Diego County DA released a Parabon Snapshot DNA-phenotype composite and announced a $52,000 combined reward. On Nov. 13, 2018, police announced that DNA comparisons and genealogical work identified David Mabrito, a transient who was 38 in 2007 and who died by suicide in 2011; an unprocessed DNA sample taken by Oceanside police during a traffic stop was matched to the crime-scene evidence (NBC 7 San Diego). Because he is dead, he was never charged; he is recorded as identified by police, never charged/convicted.
cases.solvedHow: Resolved through DNA: phenotyping (2017) narrowed the search; familial matching and an Oceanside PD sample identified the deceased suspect (2018).

cases.audioScript: On Christmas Eve, 2002, twenty-seven-year-old Laci Peterson vanished from her home in Modesto, California. She was eight months pregnant with a son the family had named Conner. Her disappearance set off one of the most-watched searches in the country. In April 2003, the remains of Laci and her unborn son washed up along the shore of San Francisco Bay, found by a woman walking her dog, near where her husband, Scott Peterson, had told police he was fishing the day she disappeared. Four days later, he was arrested. In 2004, after a six-month trial, a jury found Scott Peterson guilty of first-degree murder in Laci's death and second-degree murder in Conner's. He was sentenced to death. In 2020, the California Supreme Court overturned that death sentence over jury selection, and in 2021 he was resentenced to life without parole. His conviction still stands. In April 2026, a San Mateo County judge denied his third habeas petition in its entirety; his lawyers say they will appeal. Laci is remembered by her family as a mother-to-be who was days away from welcoming her son.
cases.summary: Laci Peterson, 27 and eight months pregnant, disappeared from the couple's Modesto, California, home on Christmas Eve 2002. In April 2003 her remains and those of her unborn son, Conner, were found washed up on the San Francisco Bay shoreline, near where Scott Peterson told police he had been fishing when she disappeared. Peterson was arrested four days after the remains were found. After a six-month trial in 2004 (moved to San Mateo County), a jury convicted him of first-degree murder for Laci and second-degree murder for Conner, and he was sentenced to death. In 2020 the California Supreme Court overturned the death sentence because the jury had been improperly screened for bias against the death penalty, while leaving the convictions in place; he was resentenced to life without parole the next year. The Los Angeles Innocence Project took up his case in 2024 and filed a third habeas petition in August 2025; on April 27, 2026, San Mateo County Superior Court Judge Elizabeth Hill denied all 14 claims. The Stanislaus County DA said the 2004 conviction has been upheld through two decades of litigation. LAIP said it would appeal.
cases.solvedHow: Convicted by jury in 2004 on circumstantial evidence (see evidence list). Conviction upheld on appeal (2020) and in habeas proceedings through April 2026.
cases.techniques: Missing-person investigation; Search of San Francisco Bay shoreline; Mitochondrial DNA comparison (hair); Forensic comparison of concrete debris; Recorded phone calls

cases.audioScript: In April 2016, San Francisco park workers found a woman buried in John McLaren Park. She was identified as Nicole Fitts. Days earlier, her family had reported both Nicole and her two-and-a-half-year-old daughter, Arianna, missing. But police soon learned that Arianna had not been seen since January or February of that year, in Oakland. Investigators say Arianna was last in the care of a babysitter and the babysitter's husband, and that Nicole was lured to meet the babysitter around the time she vanished. The FBI says it does not believe Arianna was with her mother when Nicole was killed. Nobody has been charged in Nicole's murder, and Arianna has never been found. Today, San Francisco police offer a reward of up to two hundred and fifty thousand dollars for information leading to an arrest and conviction. An SFPD sketch artist has released age progressions showing what Arianna may look like now. She was born in September 2013. If you have seen Arianna Fitts, or know what happened to her mother, call the San Francisco Police tip line at four one five, five seven five, four four four four.
cases.summary: Nicole Fitts and her daughter Arianna, then about 2 1/2, were reported missing to the San Francisco Police Department on April 5, 2016. On April 8, 2016, at about 10:30 a.m., San Francisco Recreation and Parks staff found Nicole buried in John McLaren Park; the medical examiner identified her, and SFPD investigated her death as a homicide. Investigators determined Arianna had not been seen since late February 2016 (FBI: January or February, in Oakland) and that she was last in the care of her babysitter and the babysitter's husband; SFPD says Nicole was lured to meet the babysitter around the time of her disappearance. The FBI says it believes Arianna was not with her mother when she was killed. SFPD announced a $100,000 reward and an age-progression sketch in 2020; its current case page lists a $250,000 reward. No one has been charged and Arianna remains missing.
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. SFPD Homicide and FBI joint investigation; rewards ($10,000 Best Buy, 2016; $100,000 in 2020; now $250,000); SFPD forensic age-progression sketches; public appeals.

cases.audioScript: In late August 2013, nineteen-year-old Bryce Laspisa left Sierra College in Rocklin, California, and set out on a long drive home to his family in Laguna Niguel. He was driving his mother's Toyota Highlander. Along the way he stopped in Kern County, and his family grew worried as the hours passed. At about 2:08 in the morning on August thirtieth, Bryce called his mother to say he was tired and had pulled off the road to rest. It was the last time anyone heard from him. A few hours later, around 5:30 a.m., the SUV was found near Castaic Lake in northern Los Angeles County. Bryce was not with it. Days of searching around the lake turned up no trace of him. A body found burning near the lake that September was confirmed not to be Bryce. More than a decade later, he is still missing. He was nineteen, five foot eleven, with red hair and blue eyes. If you have information about Bryce Laspisa, please call the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department at 323-890-5500.
cases.summary: Bryce Laspisa, 19, a Sierra College student, left Rocklin on Aug. 28, 2013, drove to Chico, and then began the roughly 500-mile drive to his family's home in Laguna Niguel in his mother's Toyota Highlander. On Aug. 29 he called for roadside assistance in Buttonwillow (Kern County) after running out of fuel and was later checked on by a Kern County officer, who reported he seemed fine (NBC, from his mother's account). At about 2:08 a.m. on Aug. 30 he called his mother to say he had pulled off to rest; that is the last known contact (LASD release). The 2003 Highlander was found later that morning in the Castaic Lake area of Los Angeles County — described by LASD as off Lake Hughes Road and by the LA Times as on the Main Ramp Road near the lake at about 5:30 a.m. A burned body found near the lake in September 2013 was confirmed not to be him. He remains missing; LASD asks for tips.

cases.audioScript: Just before three in the morning on April fifteenth, 2017, Humboldt State University sophomore David Josiah Lawson was at an off-campus house party on Spear Avenue in Arcata, California. As his group was leaving, a confrontation broke out in front of the house, and a fight followed. In the chaos, Josiah was stabbed. He died of his wounds. A man was arrested that morning and charged with murder, but weeks later a judge dismissed the charges, saying the evidence was not enough to go to trial, and in February 2019 a grand jury declined to indict. No one has been convicted. Josiah's mother, Charmaine Lawson, has spent years pushing for answers, and the case drew national attention on campus and beyond. The Arcata Police Department says the murder remains an open case. Investigators believe witnesses who were at that party may finally be willing to talk, and that their accounts are crucial to bringing the case back to court. A reward of up to fifty-five thousand dollars has been offered. If you were there that night, call the Arcata Police confidential tip line at seven oh seven, eight two five, twenty-five ninety.

A man was arrested and charged, but on May 5, 2017, a judge dismissed the charges for insufficient evidence; in February 2019 a grand jury declined to indict (NBC News). Arcata police describe the case as an open murder investigation and continue to appeal for witnesses. A reward of $55,000 has been publicized for information leading to an arrest. No one has been convicted.

cases.audioScript: In 1979, twelve-year-old Robin Samsoe of Huntington Beach, California, disappeared. She was later found murdered. The man convicted of killing her was Rodney James Alcala, a photographer who a year earlier had appeared as a contestant on the television show The Dating Game. Alcala was sentenced to death for Robin's murder in 1980, but that verdict was overturned. So was a second death sentence. While he waited for a third trial, DNA evidence connected him to the killings of four women in the Los Angeles area in the late 1970s: Jill Barcomb, Georgia Wixted, Charlotte Lamb and Jill Parenteau. In 2010, an Orange County jury convicted Alcala of all five murders, and a judge sentenced him to death. That same year, investigators released more than a hundred photographs found in his storage locker, asking the public to help identify the women and children in them. In 2012, he pleaded guilty in New York to murdering two more young women there in the 1970s, Cornelia Crilley and Ellen Hover. Alcala died of natural causes on California's death row in July 2021, at seventy-seven. Investigators believe there may be other victims who were never identified.
cases.summary: Rodney James Alcala was convicted in Santa Ana on February 25, 2010, of five counts of first-degree murder: the 1979 kidnapping and murder of 12-year-old Robin Samsoe of Huntington Beach and the killings of four Los Angeles-area women, Jill Barcomb (18, 1977), Georgia Wixted (27, 1977), Charlotte Lamb (32, 1978) and Jill Parenteau (21, 1979). On March 30, 2010, Judge Francisco Briseno followed the jury's recommendation and sentenced him to death (Daily Pilot/Los Angeles Times). Alcala had twice before been sentenced to death for Samsoe's murder, in 1980 and 1986; both judgments were overturned on appeal. DNA evidence linking him to the Los Angeles cases was found after the second reversal. In March 2010 the Orange County DA and Huntington Beach police released more than 100 photographs found in his Seattle storage locker and asked the public to help identify the people pictured (OCDA). On December 14, 2012, in Manhattan, Alcala pleaded guilty to the 1971 murder of Cornelia Crilley and the 1977 murder of Ellen Hover, both 23 (Los Angeles Times; DNAinfo), and was later sentenced to 25 years to life. He was known as the "Dating Game Killer" because he appeared on The Dating Game in 1978. He died of natural causes at a hospital near Corcoran, California, on July 24, 2021, aged 77 (NBC News; CBS News; BBC).
cases.solvedHow: The Samsoe case was prosecuted three times; DNA testing later tied Alcala to four Los Angeles-area murders, which were joined to the 2010 retrial. New York cold-case investigators reopened two 1970s murders and obtained guilty pleas in 2012.
cases.techniques: DNA matching (cold-case evidence); Joinder of cold cases at retrial; Public release of suspect's photographs to identify victims; Cold-case review (Manhattan DA)

cases.audioScript: In May 2010, Sam Herr's father went to check on his twenty-six-year-old son's apartment in Costa Mesa, California. Inside, he found the body of Sam's friend, twenty-three-year-old Julie Kibuishi, who had been shot. Sam was missing, and at first it looked as if he might be the killer. But withdrawals from Sam's bank account led detectives to a neighbor, a community theater actor named Daniel Wozniak. Prosecutors said Wozniak, desperate for money for his upcoming wedding, rent and debts, lured Sam, an Army veteran with about sixty-two thousand dollars saved from his service in Afghanistan, to a theater in Los Alamitos and shot him. Then he used Sam's phone to lure Julie to the apartment, killed her, and staged the scene to frame Sam. Wozniak later confessed. In December 2015, an Orange County jury convicted him of two counts of special-circumstances murder, including murder for financial gain, and in January 2016 the jury recommended the death penalty, and he was sentenced to death that September. In November 2026, California's governor announced a plan to commute all death sentences to life without parole; that move is being challenged. Sam's father said in court that the verdict confirmed what the family had always known. Sam Herr and Julie Kibuishi are remembered by their families and friends.
cases.summary: On May 21, 2010, Daniel Wozniak shot Army veteran Sam Herr, 26, in a Los Alamitos theater where Wozniak performed, then used Herr's phone to lure Juri 'Julie' Kibuishi, 23, to Herr's Costa Mesa apartment, where he shot her and staged the scene to make it appear Herr had attacked her and fled (LA Times). Herr's father found Kibuishi's body on May 22, 2010 (ABC News). Withdrawals from Herr's bank account led Costa Mesa police to Wozniak, who confessed. Prosecutors said he wanted money for his wedding, rent and debts and targeted Herr's roughly $62,000 in savings. On Dec. 16, 2015, a jury convicted Wozniak of two felony counts of special-circumstances murder (multiple murders; murder for financial gain), and on Jan. 11, 2016, recommended death (Orange County DA). The court sentenced him to death on Sept. 23, 2016 (Judge John Conley), and the case is on automatic appeal (Orange County DA). On Nov. 5, 2026, Gov. Gavin Newsom announced a plan to change all California death sentences to life without the possibility of parole; the Habeas Corpus Resource Center said sentences had not yet been formally commuted, and on Nov. 19, 2026 a coalition of prosecutors asked the California Supreme Court to halt the effort (LA Times). His exact status is therefore unsettled as of Nov. 21, 2026.
cases.solvedHow: Solved through financial records (withdrawals from Herr's account), interrogation leading to a confession, and recovery of the handgun; jury conviction in 2015.

cases.audioScript: On January thirtieth, 1989, thirteen-year-old Ilene Misheloff was walking home alone from Wells Middle School in Dublin, California. At about three in the afternoon, witnesses saw her walking on Amador Valley Boulevard near Village Parkway, and she was not seen again. Her key fob was later found near the entrance to John Mape Park, along the route she usually took home. She was wearing a charcoal gray Esprit polo sweater, a pink and charcoal striped skirt, and black low-top Keds, and she had braces and freckles. For more than thirty years, the community held a candlelight vigil and walk on the anniversary. After Ilene's mother, Maddi, died in 2020, the walk ended, but the investigation did not. On the thirty-fifth anniversary, Dublin's police chief said the department will continue to follow every tip and will not rest until the case is brought to a conclusion. Police have offered a ninety-five-thousand-dollar reward for information leading to an arrest and conviction. If you know anything, call Dublin Police Services at 925-833-6670.
cases.summary: On Jan. 30, 1989, 13-year-old Ilene Misheloff was abducted while walking home from Wells Middle School in Dublin, California. She was last seen at about 3 p.m., walking alone on Amador Valley Boulevard near Village Parkway. Her key fob was later found near the entrance to John Mape Park, along the route she normally took home. She was last seen wearing a charcoal gray Esprit polo sweater, a pink and charcoal gray horizontally striped skirt and black low-top Keds; she had braces, pierced ears, freckles and a small lump on the inside of her left ankle. For more than 30 years a community vigil and walk marked the anniversary; it ended after her mother, Maddi Misheloff, died in April 2020. On the 35th anniversary in January 2024, Dublin Police Chief Nate Schmidt said the department would continue to follow every tip, and Patch reported a $95,000 reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the person responsible. Dublin Police asks anyone with information to contact Sgt. Craig Evans at 925-833-6670; the FBI San Francisco office also accepts tips.

cases.audioScript: On Memorial Day weekend, 1996, nineteen-year-old Kristin Smart, a student here at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, went to a party near campus. Around two in the morning, she was seen on a lawn next door, and she set off to walk back to her dorm. She never made it. For decades, there was no arrest, and she was declared legally dead in 2002. Her family kept billboards up along Highway 101 so no one would forget. Then, in April 2021, San Luis Obispo County sheriff's officials arrested a former classmate, Paul Flores, who had long been called a prime suspect. Prosecutors said he killed Kristin during an attempted rape. In October 2022, a jury in Salinas convicted him of first-degree murder, and in March 2023 he was sentenced to twenty-five years to life. But Kristin's body has never been found, and investigators were still serving search warrants in 2026. If you know where she is, contact the San Luis Obispo County Sheriff's Office.
cases.summary: Kristin Smart, 19, of Stockton, a Cal Poly San Luis Obispo student, disappeared on Memorial Day weekend 1996 after an off-campus party; a party host told investigators he saw her on a neighboring lawn around 2 a.m. She was declared legally dead in 2002. Paul Flores, a Cal Poly classmate long described as a prime suspect, was arrested by San Luis Obispo County sheriff's officials on April 13, 2021. A Monterey County jury convicted him of first-degree murder in October 2022; prosecutors said Smart was killed during an attempted rape. He was sentenced on March 10, 2023 to 25 years to life. Her body has never been found; authorities served a new search warrant in May 2026.
cases.solvedHow: Solved without a body: decades of searches and warrants, renewed public attention, and a 2021 arrest led to a jury conviction on circumstantial and witness evidence.

Detectives first believed two burglars who had attacked another woman nearby were responsible. The case went cold for more than twenty years. cases.audioScript: In the 1980s, Dorothea Puente ran a boardinghouse on F Street in downtown Sacramento. To many, she seemed like a kindly grandmother. Prosecutors said she took in elderly, ill and alcoholic tenants, and then killed them for their government benefit checks. In 1988, a social worker came looking for a tenant named Bert Montoya. Puente gave her different stories, including that he had gone to Mexico. Acting on a tip from another tenant, police began to dig in the yard. In November 1988, they found seven bodies. Officers searched for Puente after the bodies were found, and she was arrested in Los Angeles. Tests found traces of a prescription sedative she often refilled in all of the bodies buried in the garden. In 1993, after a record twenty-four days of deliberation, a jury convicted her of murdering three tenants: Dorothy Miller, Benjamin Fink and Leona Carpenter. The jury could not agree on six other murder counts. She was sentenced to life in prison without parole, and she died in prison in 2011, at eighty-two.
cases.summary: Dorothea Montalvo Puente operated a boardinghouse on F Street in Sacramento in the 1980s; prosecutors said she preyed on elderly, ill and alcoholic tenants and killed them for their disability and Social Security checks. She had earlier served three years of a five-year prison term for drugging elderly people and stealing their benefit checks, and was on parole while running the boardinghouse. In 1988, a social worker checking on tenant Bert Montoya was given shifting explanations for his absence; acting on a tip from another tenant, police dug in the yard and in November 1988 found seven bodies, including Montoya's. Puente was located and arrested in Los Angeles and flown back to Sacramento on Nov. 18, 1988. Toxicology tests found Dalmane, a prescription drug Puente frequently refilled, in all of the bodies buried in the garden, and a note listing initials and dollar amounts was found in the house. She was tried on nine murder counts; the trial was held in Monterey before Judge Michael J. Virga. On Aug. 26, 1993, after 24 days of deliberation, the jury convicted her of first-degree murder of Dorothy Miller and Benjamin Fink and second-degree murder of Leona Carpenter, and deadlocked on six other counts. She was sentenced to life without parole and died in prison of natural causes on March 27, 2011, at age 82.

cases.audioScript: Between 1972 and 1973, young women hitchhiking around Santa Cruz County, California, began disappearing. They were high school and college students, ages fifteen to twenty-three. Their killer was a six-foot-nine former construction worker named Edmund Kemper. He buried some victims in the Santa Cruz mountains near Summit Road and at his home in Aptos. In 1973 he killed his own mother and her friend. Then he did something few killers do: he called Santa Cruz police from a pay phone and confessed. Kemper was convicted of eight murders and given eight concurrent life sentences. As a teenager, he had already been accused of shooting his grandparents. He has been denied parole many times since 1979. On July ninth, 2024, the board denied him again, for seven years. At that 2024 hearing, he did not attend, and the parole board found he still posed a high risk to reoffend, citing an incident in prison as recently as 2022. He will not be eligible again until 2031, when he will be eighty-two.
cases.summary: Edmund Kemper killed seven women and one girl in Santa Cruz County in 1972-1973, including female high school and college students aged 15-23, his mother and her friend. The eight murder counts at his April 30, 1973 arraignment named Mary Ann Pesce, Anita Luchessa, Aiko Koo, Cindy Schall, Rosalind Thorpe, Allison Liu, his mother Clarnell Strandberg and her friend Sally Hallett. Years earlier, at 15, he had killed his paternal grandparents. After killing his mother and her friend, he called Santa Cruz police from a phone booth in Pueblo, Colorado, confessed, and turned himself in. He was convicted in 1973 and received eight concurrent life sentences. He was denied parole on July 9, 2024 for seven years; next eligibility is 2031.

cases.audioScript: In May 2004, fifty-three-year-old Oakey Albert Kite Junior, known as Al, was living alone in his townhouse in Aurora, Colorado. That month he rented a room to a man who called himself Robert Cooper. The man said he was from the East Coast and worked for Wells Fargo Bank. On May twenty-fourth, 2004, Al was found dead in the basement of his home. He had been bound, beaten, tortured and stabbed. His wallet and cell phone were missing. Afterward, an unidentified man tried to use Al's debit card at an ATM. Investigators learned that the name, identification and contact information on the renter's application were false. The man who called himself Robert Cooper is the primary suspect, and he has never been identified. Witnesses described him as a white man, about five foot ten, around one hundred seventy to one hundred eighty pounds, with brown or black hair, and possibly an Eastern European accent. No one has been charged. If you rented a room to, worked with, or knew a man using the name Robert Cooper in 2004, contact Aurora police or the FBI.
cases.summary: Colorado's cold-case listing and Oxygen say that on May 24, 2004, the body of Oakey Albert "Al" Kite Jr., 53, was found in the basement of his residence in Aurora, Colorado; he had been bound, beaten, tortured and stabbed, and his wallet and cell phone were taken. An unidentified man attempted to use his debit card at an ATM afterward. A man who rented a room from Kite shortly before the murder, identifying himself as "Robert Cooper," claimed to be from the East Coast and to work for Wells Fargo Bank, and gave false identification and contact information on his rental application; he is the primary suspect. Witnesses described him as a white male, about 5'10", 170-180 lbs, brown or black hair, possibly with an Eastern European accent. Oxygen's coverage (The DNA of Murder with Paul Holes) gives May 24 as the date police were called; the FBI date of discovery is used here. The case is listed by the Colorado Bureau of Investigation and remains unsolved. "Robert Cooper" is an alias of an unidentified person, not a real person's name, which is why it is recorded.

cases.audioScript: On December twentieth, 1984, twelve-year-old Jonelle Matthews sang in a Christmas concert with her middle school honor choir in Greeley, Colorado. A friend's father dropped her off at home around eight that night. She was never seen alive again. For thirty-four years, Jonelle's disappearance haunted Greeley. Then, in July 2019, a pipeline crew digging in a field in rural Weld County found human remains. The coroner identified them as Jonelle. A forensic pathologist ruled her death a homicide. Police named a man who had lived about two miles from her, Steven Pankey, as a person of interest. In October 2020, a grand jury indicted him. His first trial ended with a hung jury on the main counts. At his second trial, in October 2022, a jury found him guilty of felony murder and kidnapping. A judge sentenced him to life in prison, with the possibility of parole after twenty years, under the law in place in 1984. Jonelle's parents and sister spoke in court. After almost thirty-eight years, they finally had answers about the girl who never came home from her Christmas concert.
cases.summary: Jonelle Matthews, 12, disappeared on Dec. 20, 1984, after performing in a Christmas concert with the Franklin Middle School Honor Choir in Greeley, Colorado. She was last seen about 8 p.m. when a friend and the friend's father dropped her off at home (Greeley Tribune). On July 23, 2019, a pipeline excavation crew found human remains near Weld County Roads 49 and 34 1/2; the Weld County Coroner identified them as Jonelle and a forensic pathologist determined she was a homicide victim (Greeley PD). Steven Dana Pankey was identified as a person of interest and then a suspect. A Weld County grand jury indicted him on Oct. 9, 2020, and he was arrested (Greeley PD; Greeley Tribune). His first trial in 2021 ended in a mistrial on most counts, though he was convicted of false reporting (Denver7). On Oct. 31, 2022, a jury found him guilty of felony murder and second-degree kidnapping; it found him not guilty of first-degree (after deliberation) murder. Judge Timothy G. Kerns sentenced him to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 20 years, under the statute in effect at the time of the crime (Denver7).
cases.solvedHow: Remains recovered by chance during 2019 pipeline excavation reopened the case as a homicide; Greeley PD and the Weld DA took evidence to a grand jury, which indicted Pankey. Convicted at a second trial.

cases.audioScript: On the morning of May twenty-fourth, 2019, Jennifer Dulos, a fifty-year-old mother of five here in New Canaan, Connecticut, dropped her children off at school. It was the last time anyone heard from her. She and her estranged husband, Fotis Dulos, were in a bitter divorce and custody battle. Investigators later found clothing and sponges with Jennifer's blood in trash cans in Hartford, where cameras recorded a man appearing to be Fotis dumping bags. In January 2020, Connecticut State Police charged Fotis Dulos with murder and kidnapping, and charged his girlfriend, Michelle Troconis, with conspiracy. Weeks later, Fotis Dulos died after a suicide attempt, before he could stand trial. In 2024, a jury convicted Michelle Troconis of conspiracy to commit murder, and she was sentenced to fourteen and a half years in prison. Jennifer's body has never been found. Her case led Connecticut to expand its legal definition of domestic violence. Anyone with information about where Jennifer is can contact Connecticut State Police.
cases.summary: Jennifer Farber Dulos, 50, a New Canaan mother of five, vanished on May 24, 2019; police said she was last heard from while dropping her children at school. She and her estranged husband, Fotis Dulos, were in a contentious divorce and custody battle. Court documents described clothes and sponges with her blood found in Hartford trash cans, where surveillance cameras captured a man appearing to be Fotis Dulos disposing of bags. On Jan. 7, 2020, Connecticut State Police charged Fotis Dulos with capital murder, murder and kidnapping; his girlfriend Michelle Troconis and his friend, attorney Kent Mawhinney, were charged with conspiracy to commit murder. Fotis Dulos died on Jan. 30, 2020, two days after a suicide attempt, before trial. Troconis was convicted in 2024 on six counts including conspiracy to commit murder and on May 31, 2024 was sentenced to 14 1/2 years to serve. In June 2025 prosecutors dropped the conspiracy charge against Mawhinney; he pleaded guilty to misdemeanor interfering with an officer, with time served. Jennifer Dulos's body has never been found.

cases.audioScript: On June first, 2012, nineteen-year-old Natanalie Perez, known to her family as Naty, was last seen at a motel on Southwest Eighth Street in Miami, where she was believed to be living. She had grown up and graduated from high school in Sebring, Florida, and moved to South Florida to live with a friend. Her family says she had stopped calling and texting the way she used to, and her phone went straight to voicemail. In the fall of 2012, Miami police told reporters she may have been seen at the Dolphin Mall as recently as August, and her mother and aunt handed out flyers alongside a Miami police detective. That lead did not bring her home. Her family has said they believe she was being exploited by people who controlled her, but no one has been charged. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children has released an age-progressed photo, and notes she may be with a man. Naty has a tattoo on her left wrist. If you have seen Natanalie Marie Perez, call the Miami Police Department at three oh five, six oh three, sixty-three hundred, or NCMEC at one eight hundred, the lost.

In October 2012, Miami police told NBC 6 South Florida that she had been seen at Dolphin Mall as recently as August 2012; her mother and aunt distributed flyers with Det. Jose Rojas. cases.audioScript: Early on the morning of June twenty-seventh, 1995, twenty-seven-year-old Jodi Huisentruit overslept for the first time. She was the morning anchor at KIMT-TV in Mason City, Iowa. When her producer called around four a.m., Jodi said she'd be right in. She never arrived. When police went to check on her, they found her car in the parking lot of her apartment building, and her things scattered around it: red high heels, a hair dryer, hair spray, earrings, and her car key, bent. Neighbors later said they had heard a scream. There were no cameras and no witnesses. Jodi has not been seen since. She was declared legally dead in 2001. Mason City police and the Iowa Division of Criminal Investigation say the case is anything but cold. Tips still come in, sometimes every day, and detectives travel to follow them. No one has been charged. If you know something, call Mason City police at 641-421-3636.
cases.summary: Jodi Huisentruit, 27, a morning anchor at KIMT-TV in Mason City, Iowa, vanished early on June 27, 1995. Her producer called her at about 4 a.m. when she had not arrived; she said she had overslept and would be right in (CNN; Charley Project). When she still had not arrived, police were asked to check on her. At her apartment complex parking lot they found her car and her belongings scattered around it, including red shoes, a hair dryer, hair spray, earrings and a bent car key (CNN; KCRG; Charley Project). Neighbors reported hearing a scream (Charley Project). She was declared legally dead in May 2001 (Charley Project). The Mason City Police Department and Iowa DCI continue to investigate; in 2026 the lead investigator said tips arrive weekly or even daily and that he had followed leads in about five states in the past year (KGLO). In 2025 a judge unsealed a 2017 search warrant concerning a person of interest who has since died; police said nothing useful came from it (KCRG). No one has been charged.

cases.audioScript: In the late 1970s and early 1980s, the valley where Lewiston, Idaho, meets Clarkston and Asotin, Washington, lost four young people. On April twenty-eighth, 1979, twelve-year-old Christina White vanished in Asotin during the county fair. She had called her mother that afternoon to say she felt sick from the heat. Neither Christina nor her new white ten-speed bicycle was ever found. Then, on September twelfth, 1982, stepsisters Kristina Nelson, twenty-one, and Brandy Miller, eighteen, left Kristina's Lewiston apartment to walk to a grocery store. That same night, thirty-five-year-old Steven Pearsall was dropped off at the Lewiston Civic Theatre, where he worked, to do laundry and practice his clarinet. Police later found the clarinet. None of the three came home. In March 1984, the remains of Kristina and Brandy were found down a hillside off Highway 3, about forty miles from Lewiston. Steven has never been found. In 1995, Lewiston police said they believed one man was responsible, but no one has ever been charged, and no suspect is named here. If you remember anything about the fair in 1979 or the theater in 1982, police still want to hear from you.
cases.summary: Investigators in the Lewis-Clark Valley have long linked four cases. Christina Lee White, 12, vanished in Asotin, Washington, on April 28, 1979, during the Asotin County Fair; a source on Solve the Case (Asotin County Sheriff's case 1979-18) says she called her mother at about 2:30 p.m. from a friend's house to say she felt sick from the heat. She and her bicycle were never found. On Sept. 12, 1982, stepsisters Kristina Nelson, 21, and Jacqueline "Brandy" Miller, 18, walked toward a Lewiston grocery store and disappeared; the same night Steven Pearsall, 35, a janitor at the Lewiston Civic Theatre, was dropped off there around midnight and vanished. His clarinet was found at the theater. On March 19, 1984, the remains of Nelson and Miller were found down a hillside off Highway 3 near Kendrick, about 40 miles from Lewiston; the coroner ruled the deaths homicides. Pearsall has never been found. In January 1995, Lewiston police told The Spokesman-Review they were '99 percent certain' who was responsible for the four cases, but no one has been charged. That person is living as far as public sources show and is not named here. Kristin David's 1981 murder is often compared to these cases but is filed separately (US-ID-002). cases.audioScript: On the morning of Friday, June twenty-sixth, 1981, twenty-two-year-old Kristin David set out on her blue ten-speed bicycle from Moscow, Idaho. She was a senior at the University of Idaho, studying broadcast journalism and political science, and she planned to ride south on Highway 95 to Lewiston. Witnesses later told investigators they saw a woman matching her description being approached by a man in a brown van just outside the town of Genesee. On July fourth, her remains began to be found in and along the Snake River, about six miles west of Clarkston, Washington. They had been hidden in black plastic bags, and some were wrapped in pages from April 1981 editions of the local newspaper. Her bicycle and clothing were never found. The FBI describes the man in the van as white, about thirty, around five foot ten, stocky, with a beard, driving a well-kept brown van with yellow plates. In 2021, the FBI said evidence was being retested and that the case is not cold. No one has been charged. If you saw that van on Highway 95, contact the FBI at tips dot F B I dot gov.
cases.summary: Kristin Noel David, 22, a University of Idaho senior, left Moscow, Idaho, on her blue 10-speed bicycle on June 26, 1981, heading south on U.S. Highway 95 toward Lewiston. The FBI says multiple travelers that day saw a female cyclist matching her description being approached by a man driving a brown van on the southbound side of the highway just outside Genesee. On July 4, 1981, her dismembered remains began to be found in and along the Snake River about six miles west of Clarkston, Washington, just west of Silcott Island; more were found downriver the next day. The remains were in black plastic bags, and some were wrapped in pages from April 1981 editions of the local newspaper (Fox News identifies it as the Lewiston Morning Tribune). Her bicycle, clothing and personal items were never recovered. In June 2021 the FBI Salt Lake City office released a description of the suspect (white male, about 30, about 5'10", about 180 lbs, stocky, bearded) and his van (well-kept brown van with yellow plates with dark lettering), said evidence was being retested, and said the case was not considered cold. The investigation is joint with the Asotin County Sheriff's Office and Lewiston Police. Her case is often compared to the Lewis-Clark Valley cases (US-ID-001), but investigators have not publicly linked them. No one has been charged.

cases.audioScript: In June 2017, investigators in Canyon County, Idaho, found the bodies of three people hidden in a shed on a rural property near Caldwell that Mike Bullinger had recently bought. They were Cheryl Baker, fifty-six, Nadja Medley, forty-eight, and Nadja's fourteen-year-old daughter, Payton, all from Ogden, Utah. Each had been killed by a single gunshot. Cheryl was married to the property's owner, Gerald Michael Bullinger, known as Mike. According to news reports, Nadja believed she was engaged to him. Bullinger was gone. A car connected to him was later found abandoned at the Pacific Creek Campground in Wyoming, near Grand Teton National Park, and he was reported entering the park on June eleventh. In August 2017, after DNA confirmed the identities of Nadja and Payton, Canyon County charged Bullinger with three counts of first-degree murder. A massive search followed, but he has never been found. In 2018, the sheriff said he believed Bullinger was probably dead. He has not been convicted of any crime, and the case remains open. If you have information about Mike Bullinger, contact the Canyon County Sheriff's Office.
cases.summary: On June 19, 2017, three bodies were found in a shed on a recently purchased rural property near Caldwell, Idaho, belonging to Gerald Michael "Mike" Bullinger (Jackson Hole News&Guide). The coroner identified Cheryl Baker, 56 (some reports say 57), of Ogden, Utah, through dental records on June 30, and Nadja Medley, 48, and her daughter Payton Medley, 14, also of Ogden, through DNA; each was killed by a single gunshot (Idaho News 6; KUTV). Baker was married to Gerald Michael "Mike" Bullinger; Medley was reportedly engaged to him. A car connected to Bullinger was found abandoned at the Pacific Creek Campground in Teton County, Wyoming, and police said he was seen entering Grand Teton National Park on June 11 (Jackson Hole News&Guide). In August 2017, after the DNA results, Bullinger was charged with three counts of first-degree murder. He has never been located; in June 2018, Canyon County Sheriff Kieran Donahue said he was probably dead (Salt Lake Tribune). He has not been tried or convicted.

cases.audioScript: On May twenty-ninth, 1984, thirty-one-year-old Linda Hatfield worked her shift at the Hunt Club in Garden City, Idaho. When she finished at one a.m., a bouncer walked her to her car and watched her drive off toward her home in Middleton. That was the last confirmed sighting of Linda. About an hour later, witnesses in Middleton reported seeing her T-Bird and another vehicle parked in the street, and they heard what sounded like a man and a woman arguing. At eight-thirty that morning, her car was found in a parking lot on South Curtis Road in Boise. By June fourth, investigators had found enough evidence to change her case from a missing person to a homicide. That November, her wallet and credit cards were found in the drained New York Canal. Linda's remains have never been found, and no one has been charged. In 2025, Ada County Sheriff's detectives said they were reanalyzing important evidence, and they want to know more about her missing wedding ring set and the night she disappeared. If you know anything, call the Ada County Sheriff's Office at 208-577-3102.
cases.summary: On May 29, 1984, Linda Hatfield, 31, worked her shift at the Hunt Club in Garden City, Idaho; when she finished at 1 a.m., a bouncer walked her to her car and watched her drive toward her home in Middleton, the last confirmed sighting. At about 2 a.m., witnesses in Middleton reported seeing her T-Bird and another vehicle parked in the street and hearing what they believed was a man and a woman arguing. At 8:30 a.m., her car was found in a parking lot in the 2700 block of S. Curtis Road in Boise; because she had not yet been reported missing, it was left there. After her husband reported her missing to the Canyon County Sheriff's Office on June 1, the Ada County Sheriff's Office and Boise Police processed the car, and by June 4, 1984, the case had been changed from a missing person case to a homicide. In November 1984, her wallet and credit cards were found in the recently drained New York Canal, and in June 1987 a court ruled there was clear and convincing evidence she was deceased. In 1988 a man told investigators she may have been set up to be robbed; the Ada County Sheriff's Office names Cary Burgess, who was known to frequent the Hunt Club, as a primary suspect (identified by police, never charged/convicted in this case); he arrived at a family member's house between 2 and 3 a.m. that night covered in mud, with a woman's wedding ring set, and appearing manic. Burgess was convicted of a separate July 6, 1984 abduction and rape in Boise and died in prison in 2001. Her remains have never been found. In April 2025, Ada County detectives said they were reanalyzing important items of evidence and asked for information about her missing wedding ring set, the location of her remains and the night she disappeared.

cases.audioScript: In the early morning hours of November thirteenth, 2022, four University of Idaho students were stabbed to death in an off-campus house here in Moscow. They were Madison Mogen and Kaylee Goncalves, both twenty-one, and Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin, both twenty. Two roommates survived. One later told police she saw a masked figure dressed in black walk past her and leave the house. For weeks there was no suspect, and fear spread across the campus and the town. Then investigators focused on a white Hyundai Elantra seen circling the neighborhood that night, and on a tan leather knife sheath left on one of the beds. DNA from that sheath eventually led investigators to a criminal justice graduate student at Washington State University, just across the state line in Pullman. On December thirtieth, 2022, Bryan Kohberger was arrested at his parents' home in Pennsylvania. In July 2025, to avoid the death penalty, he pleaded guilty to all four murders. He was sentenced to four consecutive life terms without parole, and he declined to say a word in court. Their families say the four are remembered for how they lived.
cases.summary: Madison Mogen, 21, Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Ethan Chapin, 20, all University of Idaho students, were stabbed to death at an off-campus home in Moscow, Idaho, in the early morning of Nov. 13, 2022. Moscow police said an edged weapon such as a knife was used and there was no sign of forced entry. A surviving roommate told investigators she saw a masked figure in black walk past her and leave the home, and surveillance footage showed a white Hyundai Elantra circling the home several times between 3:29 a.m. and 4:04 a.m. A tan leather knife sheath was found on one victim's bed; the Idaho State Lab reported on Dec. 28, 2022, that a DNA profile from trash collected by investigators identified a male who could not be excluded as the biological father of the person whose DNA was on the sheath. Bryan Kohberger, 28, a criminal justice graduate student at Washington State University in Pullman, was arrested in Pennsylvania on Dec. 30, 2022, and charged with four counts of first-degree murder and felony burglary. A grand jury indicted him in May 2023, and a judge entered not-guilty pleas on his behalf. In July 2025 he pleaded guilty to all four murders under a plea deal that spared him the death penalty, and on July 23, 2025, at the Ada County Courthouse in Boise, he was sentenced to four life terms without parole. Prosecutors said that at trial they would have used DNA, his online purchase history, surveillance video of his car and cellphone data.
cases.solvedHow: Solved by investigative genetic genealogy on touch DNA from the knife sheath, confirmed by DNA from family trash, plus car surveillance and phone records; ended in a guilty plea (no trial).

cases.audioScript: In September 2019, two children from Rexburg, Idaho, simply stopped being seen. Sixteen-year-old Tylee Ryan and her seven-year-old brother, Joshua, known as JJ, were the children of Lori Vallow. That November, worried relatives asked Rexburg police to check on JJ, and officers could not find him. By then, Lori had married Chad Daybell, an author who wrote books about the end times. His first wife, Tammy, had died in October 2019, at first believed to have died in her sleep, and the couple married on a Hawaii beach weeks later. In June 2020, after months of searching, investigators found the children's remains buried on Chad Daybell's property near Salem. Prosecutors said the killings were fueled by power, sex, money and apocalyptic beliefs. In May 2023, a jury convicted Lori Vallow Daybell, and she was sentenced to life without parole. A year later, a jury convicted Chad Daybell of all three murders, and on June first, 2024, he was sentenced to death. Tylee's brother asked that the children be remembered for who they were, not as a headline.
cases.summary: Tylee Ryan, 16, and Joshua "JJ" Vallow, 7, the children of Lori Vallow Daybell, were last seen on different days in September 2019; in late November 2019 relatives asked Rexburg police for a welfare check on JJ, and police did not find him at the family's home. Chad Daybell's first wife, Tammy Daybell, died on Oct. 19, 2019, initially believed to have died in her sleep, and Chad and Lori married in Hawaii less than three weeks later. The children's remains were found on Chad Daybell's Idaho property in June 2020 after a monthslong search. A jury convicted Lori Vallow Daybell in May 2023 of two counts of first-degree murder and three counts of conspiracy, and on July 31, 2023 she was sentenced to life in prison without parole. Chad Daybell was convicted on May 30, 2024 of first-degree murder in all three deaths, conspiracy and insurance fraud, and on June 1, 2024 Judge Steven Boyce sentenced him to death on the jury's finding. Prosecutors described the case as driven by power, sex, money and apocalyptic spiritual beliefs.
cases.solvedHow: Solved by a monthslong missing-children investigation (welfare check, searches, warrants) that led to the burial sites on Chad Daybell's property, followed by jury convictions of both spouses.

cases.audioScript: On February first, 2010, Navy Seaman Kyle Antonacci was found dead in his barracks room at Naval Station Great Lakes, north of Chicago. He was twenty-two, an explosive ordnance disposal trainee from Long Island, New York. Months earlier, Kyle had been a key witness in a rape case against another sailor. He later admitted he had not told investigators everything about that night, and he became the subject of a perjury investigation. According to the Defense Department's Inspector General, Kyle was found about three hours after he walked out of an interview with the Naval Criminal Investigative Service. The Armed Forces Medical Examiner ruled his death a suicide, by hanging. His family never accepted that. They told reporters he had injuries, including a broken nose, and that the Navy first gave them a different explanation of how he died. A former Lake County coroner later said he believed Kyle was killed. In 2014, the Inspector General found that NCIS had not fully met its own standards in the rape, perjury and death investigations, but found no evidence of a conspiracy and did not overturn the suicide ruling. Officially, the case is closed. For Kyle's family, the questions remain.
cases.summary: Seaman Kyle Antonacci, 22, an explosive ordnance disposal trainee from Long Island, N.Y., was found hanging in his barracks room at Naval Station Great Lakes, Illinois, on February 1, 2010. He had been a prosecution witness in a court-martial rape case arising from a May 2009 barracks party, later admitted he had not disclosed that he also had sex with the woman that night, and was the subject of an NCIS perjury investigation at the time of his death (Navy Times; Los Angeles Times). The DoD Inspector General's evaluation (DODIG-2015-007, Nov. 3, 2014) says he was found deceased about three hours after leaving the NCIS office following a February 1, 2010 interrogation, and that the case agent did not document releasing him to his command. The Armed Forces Medical Examiner's opinion was that the manner of death was suicide. The Inspector General found that the rape, perjury and death investigations were not conducted in full compliance with NCIS standards and that a threat Antonacci reported was not thoroughly investigated, but concluded the death-investigation deficiencies did not materially affect the suicide opinion and found nothing to suggest a conspiracy. His family disputes the ruling; ABC News (2011) reported they said the Navy first told them he died in a car crash and did not tell them about injuries including a broken nose. The Los Angeles Times (2013) reported that the former Lake County coroner said he was denied access to key evidence, was pressured to call it a suicide, and believed Antonacci was murdered. No one has been charged in connection with his death. Other people involved in the underlying 2009 rape case are not named here.
cases.solvedHow: Officially resolved as a suicide by the Armed Forces Medical Examiner. Review steps: NCIS death investigation, AFME autopsy and opinion, and a DoD Inspector General evaluation in 2014.
