cases.audioScript: On July fifth, 1996, Everett Thompson was at work at the restaurant he owned on Chicago's South Side when his wife, Lydia, called him, frantic. She said her brother, Kenneth White, who had moved in with the family months earlier after his release from prison, had chased her around the house with an ax, and she had locked herself in a bedroom. Everett left work to go home. He, Lydia, and their sons, eleven-year-old Everett Junior and eight-year-old Andrew, were never seen again. Kenneth White told people the family had gone on vacation. Investigators later learned he had forged documents to sell the family's home, and that the house had been altered after their disappearance. In December 1997, while White was held on a federal bank fraud charge, a prosecutor told a judge the government believed he had killed the family. He was never charged with murder. On Christmas Day, 1997, White died by suicide in custody. Chicago police called him their top suspect. The Thompsons have never been found. If you have any information about Everett, Lydia, Everett Junior or Andrew, contact Chicago police.
cases.summary: Everett Thompson Sr., 40, owned a restaurant in Chicago's Park Manor neighborhood; he and his wife Lydia, 43, lived with their sons Everett Jr., 11, and Andrew, 8, in the 8100 block of South Rhodes Avenue in Chatham (Charley Project; Chicago Tribune). Lydia's brother Kenneth White had moved in after his release from prison. On July 5, 1996, Lydia called Everett at work, frantic, saying White had chased her with an ax; Everett left and the family was not seen again (Charley Project, citing Chicago police and NWI Times). White told various stories about a family vacation, forged documents to sell the house, and the house was found altered. In December 1997, while White was detained on a federal bank-fraud complaint, Assistant U.S. Attorney Jacqueline Ross told a magistrate judge that the circumstances showed he had killed the family; the judge noted he was not charged with murder (Chicago Tribune, Dec. 24, 1997). White died by suicide in federal custody (the Tribune reports the suicide happened on Christmas 1997) on Dec. 25, 1997, and Chicago police described him as their top suspect (Chicago Tribune, Jan. 8, 1998). He is recorded as identified by police, never charged/convicted. The family has never been found; the Cook County Sheriff lists all four as missing.

cases.audioScript: Two days after Christmas in 1956, fifteen-year-old Barbara Grimes and her younger sister Patricia, twelve or thirteen, left home on Chicago's South Side to see Elvis Presley in Love Me Tender at the Brighton Theater. Their older sister and a brother were to meet them at a bus stop after the film. The girls never showed up. What followed became one of the largest missing person searches in Cook County history. Hundreds of officers searched. Elvis himself asked the girls to go home. On January twenty-second, 1957, a motorist spotted their bodies beside a rural road near Willow Springs, southwest of the city. Investigators questioned many people over the years. A man who confessed later took it back, and no case against anyone ever held. No one has been convicted. Almost seventy years later, the Cook County Sheriff's Office still lists the Grimes sisters as an open case. If you know anything, the Sheriff's Office takes tips online.
cases.summary: On December 28, 1956, Barbara Grimes, 15, and her sister Patricia, 12 or 13 (sources differ), left their family's McKinley Park home to see the Elvis Presley film 'Love Me Tender' at the Brighton Theater. They did not come home, and they were reported missing to Chicago Police (Cook County Sheriff; NBC News; A&E). The search became one of the most labor-intensive missing person cases in Cook County history, with hundreds of officers involved and an appeal from Elvis Presley (NBC News). On January 22, 1957, their bodies were found beside a rural road near Willow Springs; the Sheriff lists the location as German Church Road and County Line Road (Cook County Sheriff; CBS Chicago; A&E). Several people were questioned. A man who signed a confession in January 1957 later recanted, saying it was coerced, and was released; accounts differ on whether he was ever formally charged (A&E says charges filed in the case were dropped for lack of proof; NBC News says he was never formally charged). The Sheriff's Office continues to accept tips. No one has been convicted.
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. 1950s techniques: mass door-to-door canvass, dredging of canals and rivers, flyers, public appeals, and polygraph-era interrogations. The Cook County Sheriff's cold case unit continues to review tips.
cases.techniques: Large-scale search and canvass; Public appeals (including by Elvis Presley); Interrogations and confessions (later recanted); Cold case review by the Cook County Sheriff

cases.audioScript: In December 1978, fifteen-year-old Robert Piest of Des Plaines, Illinois, disappeared, and witnesses said he was last seen talking with a local building contractor named John Wayne Gacy. Gacy was known in his community for performing as a clown at parties. Police obtained a search warrant for his home in unincorporated Norwood Park Township, just outside Chicago. Under the house, in the crawl space, investigators found the remains of victim after victim. In all, Gacy killed thirty-three teenage boys and young men between 1972 and 1978. In March 1980 a jury convicted him of thirty-three murders, and on May tenth, 1994, he was executed. Decades later, the Cook County Sheriff reopened the case to put names to the unidentified. Using genetic genealogy, in 2021 they identified one victim as Francis Wayne Alexander. Five victims still have no names. If a male relative of yours went missing in the 1970s, the Cook County Sheriff's Office is asking for a DNA sample.
cases.summary: John Wayne Gacy killed 33 teenage boys and young men in the Chicago area from 1972 to 1978; most remains were found in the crawl space of his unincorporated Norwood Park Township home. The investigation began after 15-year-old Robert Piest of Des Plaines disappeared on Dec. 11, 1978, and witnesses reported last seeing him with Gacy. Gacy was convicted of 33 murders in March 1980 and executed on May 10, 1994. In 2011 the Cook County Sheriff reopened efforts to identify eight unnamed victims; three have since been identified, including Francis Wayne Alexander in 2021 through genetic genealogy with the DNA Doe Project. Five victims remain unidentified, and the Sheriff has DNA profiles from all five for comparison with relatives.
cases.solvedHow: Solved in December 1978 when the Robert Piest missing-person investigation focused on Gacy; surveillance and search warrants uncovered remains under his house. Since 2011, DNA and genetic genealogy have been used to name unidentified victims.

cases.audioScript: On February 13th, 2017, two best friends, thirteen-year-old Abby Williams and fourteen-year-old Libby German, went for a walk on the Monon High Bridge Trail in Delphi, Indiana. They never came home. The next day, searchers found both girls near the trail. Libby had used her phone to record a man on the bridge, and that recording, with a few chilling words, became one of the most recognized pieces of evidence in Indiana history. For years, the case stayed unsolved, and the man in the video was known only as Bridge Guy. In October 2022, Indiana State Police arrested Richard Allen of Delphi. In November 2024, a jury found him guilty of murder, and in December he was sentenced to one hundred thirty years in prison, the maximum. Prosecutors credited Libby for having the courage to record, and Abby for hiding the phone so investigators could find it. Allen's conviction is now under appeal, and the Indiana Court of Appeals heard arguments in September 2026. Abby and Libby are remembered by their families and by a community that put up orange porch lights in their memory. Their families and neighbors have also worked to build a memorial park for them near Delphi.
cases.summary: Abby Williams (13) and Libby German (14) were dropped off near the Monon High Bridge Trail outside Delphi on the afternoon of Feb 13, 2017 and did not return. Their bodies were found the next day about half a mile east of the bridge. Libby had recorded video and audio on her phone of a man walking toward them; police released a still image, then audio of the man saying 'Down the hill.' The man was nicknamed 'Bridge Guy.' Years of tips and releases followed, including a new sketch in 2019. In 2022 investigators found a misfiled tip about Richard Allen. He was arrested Oct 26, 2022 and charged with murder. After a trial that opened Oct 18, 2024, a jury found him guilty in November 2024, and Judge Fran Gull sentenced him to 130 years on Dec 20, 2024, vacating duplicate felony-murder counts. The Indiana Court of Appeals heard his appeal Sept 21, 2026; a decision is pending as of the sources checked.
cases.solvedHow: A tip naming Richard Allen from 2017 had been misfiled; a volunteer file clerk's review in 2022 led investigators back to him. Prosecutors then tied him to the case through phone video, the unspent bullet, vehicle evidence, witness accounts and his own statements.
cases.techniques: Tip-line review (misfiled 2017 tip rediscovered in Sept 2022); Digital forensics on the victim's phone (video/audio); Firearms/ballistics comparison of an unspent round; Surveillance video and vehicle registration records; Witness and custodial statements

cases.audioScript: On Good Friday, April first, 1988, eight-year-old April Tinsley was playing with friends in Fort Wayne, Indiana. She went to get her umbrella, and she never came home. Three days later, a jogger found her body in a ditch near Spencerville. For thirty years, her killer was a mystery. Beginning in 1990, someone left chilling notes around Fort Wayne, bragging about the crime and threatening other children. Investigators saved the DNA from those notes and from the scene, and in 2015 and 2016 they released composite sketches built from that DNA. Then, in 2018, detectives sent the profile to a genetic genealogy company. Genealogist CeCe Moore used a public DNA database to trace the profile to two brothers. Detectives collected a discarded sample, the DNA matched, and on July 15th, 2018, they arrested John Miller of Grabill. He confessed, pleaded guilty that December, and was sentenced to eighty years. April's case became one of the early cold cases in America solved with this technique. April was eight years old, a choir member and a second-grader, and her community never stopped saying her name.
cases.summary: April Tinsley was abducted in Fort Wayne on April 1, 1988 and found dead April 4 in a ditch west of Spencerville. Between 1990 and 2004 an anonymous person left notes in the Fort Wayne area claiming responsibility and threatening more crimes; DNA on items left with the 2004 notes matched the crime-scene profile. In 2015 Parabon NanoLabs produced a DNA 'Snapshot' composite; in May 2018 a Fort Wayne detective submitted the DNA for genetic genealogy. CeCe Moore used GEDmatch to narrow the family to two brothers by July 2, 2018. Detectives confirmed a match using DNA from discarded trash, approached John D. Miller on July 15, 2018, and he confessed. Charged with murder, child molestation and confinement, he pleaded not guilty July 19, pleaded guilty Dec 7, 2018, and was sentenced Dec 21, 2018 to 80 years.
cases.solvedHow: Forensic genetic genealogy: the crime-scene DNA profile was uploaded to GEDmatch by Parabon NanoLabs; genealogist CeCe Moore built family trees to identify two brothers, and a covert DNA comparison confirmed the match.
cases.techniques: Forensic genetic genealogy (GEDmatch / Parabon NanoLabs); DNA phenotyping composite sketch (2015, updated 2016); Covert DNA sample from discarded trash for confirmation; Linkage of 1990-2004 taunting notes by DNA

cases.audioScript: On the evening of Friday, July seventh, 1972, twenty-six-year-old Phyllis Bailer left Indianapolis with her three-year-old daughter, headed for Bluffton to visit her parents. They never arrived. The next morning, Phyllis's car was found abandoned on Interstate 69 in Grant County, hood up. About an hour later, a woman driving in Allen County found Phyllis in a ditch beside a country road. Her little girl was alive and unharmed. Phyllis had been shot and sexually assaulted. In 1972, DNA testing didn't exist. Over the years, a partial DNA profile was developed from her clothing, and in 2024 the Indiana State Police lab produced a much stronger one. Working with a forensic genealogy company in California, the ISP Cold Case Unit identified the killer in early 2025: Fred Lienemann, a man with a long criminal record and no known connection to Phyllis. He had been murdered in Detroit in 1985, so he could never be tried. State police said that if he were alive, he would have been charged. For Phyllis's family, after fifty-three years, there are finally answers.
cases.summary: Phyllis Bailer, 26, left Indianapolis around 8 p.m. on July 7, 1972, with her 3-year-old daughter, bound for Bluffton. Her car was found abandoned northbound on I-69 in Grant County the next morning. About an hour later a driver near West and Shoaff Roads in Allen County found Phyllis dead and her daughter unharmed. The autopsy found a gunshot wound and sexual assault. A partial DNA profile was developed from her clothing in later years; in 2024 ISP's lab developed a stronger profile and, with Identifinders International, genealogists identified Fred Allen Lienemann in early 2025. He had a long criminal history and was murdered in Detroit in 1985. ISP announced the finding April 16, 2025, stating he would have been charged by the Allen County Prosecutor had he been alive.
cases.solvedHow: ISP's Cold Case Unit re-tested clothing as DNA technology improved, then partnered with Identifinders International to run forensic genetic genealogy, identifying the DNA contributor as Fred Allen Lienemann.
cases.techniques: Re-testing of preserved clothing with newer DNA methods; Forensic genetic genealogy (Identifinders International); Criminal-history and death records review

cases.audioScript: On the night of August sixth, 1975, seventeen-year-old Laurel Jean Mitchell finished her shift at a snack bar at the Epworth Forest church camp in North Webster, Indiana. She set off on foot to meet friends at a nearby amusement park, and she was never seen alive again. The next morning, two fishermen found her body in the Elkhart River, many miles away. The autopsy showed she had fought hard to survive. Her clothing and belongings were saved, and for nearly fifty years, investigators kept working. New DNA testing on that clothing, and tips from people who said they'd heard boasts about the crime, led Indiana State Police to two men. In February 2023, Fred Bandy Junior and John Lehman were arrested. In October 2024, a judge found Bandy guilty of first-degree murder and sentenced him to life in prison. Lehman received eight years for conspiracy. Laurel's sister said she felt relief, after a long road. Laurel was a dancer, a friend, and a daughter whose parents never learned what happened. Forty-nine years later, her family finally has an answer.
cases.summary: Laurel Jean Mitchell, 17, was dropped off at the Epworth Forest church camp snack bar on Aug 6, 1975. Around 10 p.m. she was seen walking toward Adventureland Amusement Park and was not seen again. A missing-person report was filed at 4:16 a.m. Aug 7 and her body was found at 10:30 a.m. in the Elkhart River near the Mallard Roost access. The autopsy found drowning and signs of a violent struggle. Her clothing was preserved. Tips in 2013, 2014 and 2019 described admissions by two men; resubmitted clothing yielded a male DNA profile (certificate Feb 2020). A voluntary DNA sample from Bandy in Dec 2022 produced a Jan 2023 result stating he was 13 billion times more likely than an unknown person to be the contributor. ISP and the Noble County Sheriff arrested Bandy and Lehman on Feb 6, 2023. Lehman was sentenced to 8 years (Oct 11, 2024). Bandy was convicted in a bench trial Oct 7, 2024, received life on Oct 22, 2024, and the Indiana Court of Appeals upheld the conviction in July 2025.
cases.solvedHow: Preserved clothing was re-tested with modern DNA methods, and long-standing tips about admissions pointed investigators to two men; a voluntary DNA sample matched the profile and arrests followed.
cases.techniques: Long-term evidence preservation; Modern STR DNA testing (ISP Laboratory Division); Voluntary DNA sample comparison; Cold-case tip development (2013-2019); Vehicle records review

cases.audioScript: Between 1987 and 1990, a killer moved along Interstate 65, striking at night-shift motel clerks. In February 1987, Vicki Heath was murdered at a Super 8 in Elizabethtown, Kentucky. On March third, 1989, Peggy Gill was killed at the Days Inn in Merrillville, Indiana, and the same night, Jeanne Gilbert was taken from the Days Inn in Remington. In January 1990, another clerk in Columbus, Indiana, was attacked, but she survived and gave police an excellent description. For more than thirty years, detectives chased leads across the country. Ballistics linked the Indiana murders, and DNA linked the others. In 2019, Indiana State Police asked the FBI for help, and investigators used investigative genetic genealogy. A close relative's DNA led to Harry Edward Greenwell, who died in 2013. In April 2022, police announced that Greenwell was responsible. He was never charged, but for the families of Vicki, Peggy, and Jeanne, and for the survivor, the question of who was finally had an answer. Jeanne's daughter said her family was grateful to every agency that never gave up.
cases.summary: Vicki Heath (41) was murdered Feb 21, 1987 at a Super 8 in Elizabethtown, Kentucky. On March 3, 1989, Peggy Gill (24) was murdered at the Days Inn in Merrillville, and Jeanne Gilbert (34) was abducted from the Days Inn in Remington and found dead near Brookston. On Jan 2, 1990 a clerk at the Days Inn in Columbus, Indiana was sexually assaulted and stabbed but escaped. ISP lab work matched ballistic evidence in the Gill and Gilbert killings and DNA linking the Heath and Gilbert murders to the Columbus assault. In 2019 ISP requested FBI GRIT help; investigative genealogy matched a close relative of Harry Edward Greenwell (born Dec 9, 1944; died January 2013 in New Albin, Iowa) with >99% probability. ISP and FBI announced the result April 5, 2022; investigators believe Greenwell may be responsible for additional crimes along I-65 from Gary to Mobile, Alabama (ISP spokesperson, ABC).
cases.solvedHow: Preserved biological and ballistic evidence plus investigative genetic genealogy (FBI GRIT) identified Greenwell via a close family match; investigators then built a movement timeline.
cases.techniques: Ballistics comparison; DNA profiling of preserved evidence; Investigative genetic genealogy (FBI GRIT); Records and newspaper-archive timeline reconstruction

cases.audioScript: Andi Wagner was twenty-four years old when her family last heard from her. On August sixth, 2022, she left her family's home in Evansville, Indiana, with an overnight bag. She called her mother in Texas about possibly moving away, and she spoke briefly with her sister. Then the calls stopped. Her family reported her missing on August twelfth. Andi had been struggling with addiction, but those who love her say she was working hard to get better, and she had planned to join her mother in Texas. Her mother, Elane, moved to Evansville to search for her daughter, and she passed away in December 2023 without answers. In May 2024, Evansville police, state police, and the FBI searched three locations in and near Oakland City after a tip. Nothing has been announced publicly since. A twenty-five-thousand-dollar reward is being offered. Andi has brown hair and brown eyes and several tattoos. If you know anything, please contact the Evansville Police Department or the FBI. Andi's family says it is time for her to come home.
cases.summary: Andi Wagner, 24, was staying with family in Evansville. On Aug 6, 2022 she packed an overnight bag, spoke to her sister, and called her mother in Texas about possibly leaving Evansville. Her family reported her missing to Evansville police on Aug 12, 2022. She was last reported seen in the Oakland City area and has ties to Newburgh. In May 2024, EPD, ISP and the FBI searched three locations in and near Oakland City on a tip and collected evidence; no public findings followed. A reward rose to $25,000 in July 2024. As of Aug 2025 (three-year mark) 14 News reported no sign of her.

cases.audioScript: Ja'Niyah McMichael was thirteen years old when she was reported missing from Gary, Indiana, on August twelfth, 2024. She is five foot four, about one hundred ten pounds, and was last seen wearing black pajama pants, a black hooded sweatshirt, and red and black shoes. Today, the FBI and Gary police believe she may be the victim of foul play. A Silver Alert was issued in September 2024, and investigators executed a search warrant in October. Her grandmother, Dalia Guerrero, has spent months searching abandoned buildings, schools, and empty lots, handing out flyers and holding vigils at the corner of Twenty-first and Broadway. At the one-year mark in August 2025, she said, someone knows something. A thirty-thousand-dollar reward is now offered for information leading to Ja'Niyah's return and the arrest and conviction of those responsible. Her family held a balloon release to celebrate her fifteenth birthday. Anyone with information, no matter how small, can call 1-800-CALL-FBI or submit a tip at tips dot fbi dot gov. Ja'Niyah's family just wants to bring her home.
cases.summary: Ja'Niyah McMichael was reported missing by her mother on Aug 12, 2024 from Gary. The FBI and Gary Police say they believe she may be a victim of foul play and have an active investigation. A Silver Alert was issued Sept 5, 2024; Gary police said detectives obtained a search warrant with the FBI in Oct 2024. The initial reward ($10,000 FBI + $10,000 City of Gary) grew to $30,000 with an anonymous donor. Family and volunteers have searched abandoned buildings, schools, undeveloped land and areas near water without new clues (FOX 32, Feb 2026). A balloon release marked her 15th birthday.

cases.audioScript: On the evening of May twelfth, 2022, the 1200 block of North Huey Street in South Bend, Indiana, was full of life. Kids were riding bikes, neighbors were enjoying the warm weather, and fifty-three-year-old Johnnie Lee Johnson was doing what he loved: washing a car. Many people in the neighborhood knew him by his nickname, Car Wash. Around eight o'clock, shots were fired, and Johnnie died in front of his home. His wife and young son were inside. Police say several people saw what happened, and the shooting was captured on video, but no one has come forward with the information detectives need. The suspect vehicle was described as a gray or silver midsize SUV, seen heading north on Huey Street. Lieutenant Kayla Miller of the South Bend Police Department says silence is not acceptable. She says a father was murdered in front of his family, and the community should speak up. Michiana Crime Stoppers is offering a reward of up to twenty-five hundred dollars for tips leading to an arrest. Tips can be anonymous. Johnnie's family is still waiting for justice.

cases.audioScript: Oolitic, Indiana, is a small town in Lawrence County, and in late February 2023, a quiet camper on the edge of town became the center of a homicide investigation. Around one in the afternoon on February twenty-fourth, forty-two-year-old James Stewart was found dead of a gunshot wound inside his camper near Lafayette Avenue. The first call suggested something else, but deputies quickly noticed inconsistencies that pointed toward foul play, and Indiana State Police crime scene technicians spent days processing the scene. James had lived most of his life in Bloomington and had only recently moved to Oolitic. Investigators say they have interviewed many people, reviewed phone records, and continue testing evidence as technology improves, but they need help. They are asking anyone who was near Salt Creek, Lafayette Avenue, or Oolitic Road in the late hours before he was found to speak up, even if you have already talked with police. You can call the Lawrence County Sheriff's Office or leave an anonymous tip with Crime Stoppers of Central Indiana.
cases.summary: James Stewart, 42, was found shot to death inside his camper near Lafayette Avenue in Oolitic on Feb. 24, 2023 (WBIW; Herald-Times). A March 2024 WISH-TV photo caption said 2024, but the Herald-Times and WBIW both give 2023, and Feb. 24, 2023 was the Friday WBIW describes. The initial 911 call suggested a possible suicide; deputies noted inconsistencies and treated it as a homicide, and ISP crime-scene technicians spent several days processing the camper and wooded area. The Sheriff's Office brought in Crime Stoppers of Central Indiana in March 2024, about a year after the killing; Crime Stoppers offers up to $1,000 (Herald-Times). WBIW (Feb 2026) says hundreds of hours have been spent on phone records, social media, GPS data, DNA and ballistics, with dozens of interviews, and asks anyone near Salt Creek, Lafayette Ave or Oolitic Road the night of Feb 23-24 to come forward. Tips: Det. Andrea Tedrow, Lawrence County Sheriff's Office, 812-275-3316, or anonymously via Crime Stoppers of Central Indiana, 317-262-TIPS (8477) (WBIW, Feb. 26, 2026).

cases.audioScript: On Wednesday, February fifteenth, 2023, twenty-one-year-old Taylor Miller was on a plumbing service call on Indianapolis's west side. Just before one-thirty in the afternoon, near North Somerset Avenue in the Haughville neighborhood, Taylor was shot. Police found two men wounded. Taylor died at the hospital that evening. His mother has worked to keep his case in the public eye, and in February 2026, IMPD confirmed a new detective had been assigned to the investigation. Detectives say they are following every lead, and they are asking for help. If you saw or heard anything on Somerset Street that afternoon, or have video from that day, please contact the IMPD Homicide Office or leave an anonymous tip with Crime Stoppers of Central Indiana. cases.audioScript: Lauren Spierer was a twenty-year-old Indiana University student from Scarsdale, New York. In the early hours of June third, 2011, she spent the night out in Bloomington with friends, including time at Kilroy's Sports Bar. Around four-thirty that morning, she was last seen walking south near North College Avenue and West Eleventh Street, headed toward her apartment. She never arrived. Over the following days and years, searchers combed lakes, forests, and fields, and the FBI searched a property in Martinsville, in Morgan County, in January 2016. No definitive evidence has ever been found. Her parents believe she is no longer alive and have offered a substantial reward. In June 2026, fifteen years later, the Bloomington Police Department said the case is still very active, with twenty-three new tips in the past year leading to multiple interviews. Lauren's family says it will never stop searching for answers. If you have any information, no matter how small it may seem, contact the Bloomington Police Department or visit findlauren dot com. Lauren is remembered for her smile, her energy, and her zest for life, and she is still missing.

A major search followed, including areas outside Bloomington; the FBI searched a Martinsville (Morgan County) property on January 28, 2016. No one has been charged. Her parents offered a $250,000 reward in 2012 (Wikipedia) and believe she is no longer alive. cases.audioScript: On Friday, November seventeenth, 1978, four young employees were closing the Burger Chef restaurant on Crawfordsville Road in Speedway, Indiana. Jayne Friedt, twenty, the assistant manager, and three teenagers, Ruth Shelton, Daniel Davis, and Mark Flemmonds, were working that night. Just after midnight, a coworker stopped by and found the back door open, the manager's office in disarray, and the staff gone. About five hundred eighty dollars had been taken. On Sunday, the bodies of all four were found in a wooded area in Johnson County. For decades, detectives followed leads across the country. Investigators say the early scene was not preserved the way it would be today, and the restaurant reopened soon afterward. Indiana State Police now say they are focused on a group of people who were committing restaurant robberies at the time. A reward was offered then, and the case has drawn books, podcasts, and documentaries. No one has ever been charged. The four were young workers just doing their jobs. State police are still asking anyone with information to come forward. The families have waited more than forty-eight years for answers.
cases.summary: Four Burger Chef employees were abducted from the Speedway restaurant at 5725 Crawfordsville Road between about 11 p.m. Nov 17, 1978 and midnight; $581 was taken. An off-duty employee found the back door open just after midnight. Jayne Friedt's car was found near the Speedway Police Department. On Nov 19 the bodies were found in rural Johnson County: two had been shot with a .38-caliber firearm, one had been stabbed, and one died of head injuries. Burger Chef Systems offered a $25,000 reward. The scene was cleaned and the restaurant reopened without photographs, an officer later admitted (Wikipedia). In 1984 an inmate gave a confession that he later recanted; it did not lead to charges (Wikipedia). ISP says it has focused on a group of people committing restaurant robberies at the time. The case has been the subject of books, podcasts and documentaries including 'The Speedway Murders' (2024).
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. ISP has said it hopes forensic technology not available in 1978 will help; it continues to ask for tips.

cases.audioScript: In the spring of 1992, a killer drove west along Interstate 70, striking small stores where employees were working alone. On April eighth, twenty-six-year-old Robin Fuldauer was shot while working at a Payless shoe store on Pendleton Pike in Indianapolis. Three days later, Patricia Smith and Patricia Magers were killed at a bridal shop in Wichita, Kansas. On April twenty-seventh, Michael McCown was killed in his mother's ceramics shop in Terre Haute, Indiana. On May third, Nancy Kitzmiller was killed at a shoe store in St. Charles, Missouri, and on May seventh, Sarah Blessing was killed at her shop in Raytown, Missouri. Ballistics showed the same twenty-two-caliber pistol was used in all six killings. Little money was taken, and investigators believe the killer was targeting petite women with long brown hair; McCown was likely mistaken for a woman. Composite sketches were released, and in 2021, age-progressed versions. St. Charles police are offering a twenty-five-thousand-dollar reward, and say they have never given up. The case has no named suspect, and the six victims are remembered by their families.
cases.summary: Six people working in small stores were shot in the back of the head between April 8 and May 7, 1992 in Indianapolis, Wichita, Terre Haute, St. Charles and Raytown. Ballistics linked the killings to the same .22-caliber pistol; police believe an Erma Werke ET22 or similar. Little cash was taken and investigators doubt robbery was the primary motive. Composite sketches were produced and age-progressed images released in 2021 (Wikipedia). A $25,000 reward is offered via St. Charles police. Possible links to two Texas killings (1993) and a 2001 Terre Haute murder were investigated; none confirmed. Several suspects were ruled out. No suspect has been publicly named.
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. Techniques used so far: ballistics linkage across four police agencies, eyewitness composites, age-progression imagery, reward and public appeals, TV coverage (Unsolved Mysteries, America's Most Wanted, People Magazine Investigates).

cases.audioScript: On the afternoon of January eighteenth, 1973, twenty-six-year-old Ann Kline was grading papers at the Old Vanderburgh County Courthouse in Evansville, Indiana. Ann was a math teacher at Lockyear College across the street, and a fire at the school had temporarily moved her class into the courthouse basement. Around three o'clock, a student stopped by to ask about a grade. A few minutes later, someone heard screaming. Ann was found in the basement hallway, fatally stabbed. Police say she was not robbed, which suggests she may have known her attacker, and they believe there may have been more than one person involved. The weapon was never found. Detectives have worked the case for over fifty years, and around 2008 said they had a break, but no one has been charged. Ann's sister Jane spoke publicly for the first time in 2024, hoping for justice. She remembers Ann as playful and full of life. Evansville police say the case remains open and active. If you know anything, call the Evansville Police Detective Unit at eight one two, four three six, seven nine seven nine.
cases.summary: Ann Kline, 26, was killed on Jan 18, 1973 in the basement level of the Old Vanderburgh County Courthouse, where her class had been temporarily relocated after a fire at nearby Lockyear College. A student who also worked as a custodian visited her classroom around 3 p.m., then heard screaming minutes later and found her. She was fatally stabbed; her purse and belongings were not taken. The knife was never found. EPD says several persons of interest were ruled out. In 2009 and 2013 14 News and NBC reported that a former lead detective was confident about an unnamed suspect and wanted to take the case to the prosecutor, but no charges followed. Detective Dillon Powers told Dateline in 2024 the case remains open and under active investigation. The Deck (audiochuck) featured the case as the 8 of Hearts.

cases.audioScript: On the morning of Friday, August seventeenth, 1984, twenty-eight-year-old Darlene Hulse was getting her three young daughters ready for the day at her home near Argos, Indiana. Around nine-thirty, a man knocked at the door. Witnesses described him as white, in his twenties, with combed-over blond hair, clean shaven, with a long face and a long nose. He forced his way in. Darlene told her two older daughters to run, and they ran to their grandparents' house for help. When officers arrived, Darlene was gone. The next day, a timber surveyor found her body in a wooded area about six miles west of her home. The man was seen driving a rusty, greenish, seventies-style four-door car, possibly a Pontiac or Oldsmobile, which has never been found. Investigators have a partial male DNA profile from her clothing. The Indiana State Police Cold Case Unit continues to investigate, and her daughters and the podcast The Deck Investigates have called for more testing. If you know anything, contact the Indiana State Police cold case hotline. Darlene's family has waited more than forty years.
cases.summary: On Aug 17, 1984, a man knocked at Darlene Hulse's rural home near Argos around 9:30 a.m., forced his way in and attacked her; two daughters escaped to relatives while the youngest, an infant, was left unharmed. The man took Darlene away in a 1970s-style four-door car, described as greenish and rusty, possibly a Pontiac or Oldsmobile. Her body was found Aug 18 by a timber surveyor in woods off Olive Trail about six miles west; the autopsy ruled it a homicide by blunt-force trauma. Police examined several suspects in 1984 and ruled them out. ISP holds more than four dozen items of evidence, including a partial male DNA profile from her clothing (prosecutor's 2023 statement; podcast). The Deck Investigates (audiochuck) launched a series in 2023 urging new testing; the prosecutor publicly disputed the podcasters' characterization. ABC57 reported a renewed ISP appeal in Aug 2025 using new technology.
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. ISP's Cold Case Unit is re-examining evidence with newer forensic technology; family and podcasters have urged further DNA testing, which could support genetic genealogy.

cases.audioScript: This pin marks a memorial in Willard Park, Indianapolis, for Sylvia Likens. Sylvia was sixteen, a girl from Lebanon, Indiana, who babysat, did odd jobs and loved the Beatles. In the summer of 1965 her parents, who worked the carnival circuit, left Sylvia and her sister as paying boarders with a woman named Gertrude Baniszewski on the city's east side. Over the next three months Sylvia was starved, beaten and abused inside that house, by adults and by neighborhood children. Neighbors later said they heard screams but did not call for help. Sylvia died on October twenty-sixth, 1965. In May 1966 a Marion County jury convicted Gertrude Baniszewski of first-degree murder, and her daughter and three teenage boys were also convicted. After an appeal, she was convicted again in 1971. Sylvia's death is credited with Indiana's law that requires every person who suspects child abuse to report it. A child advocacy center in Lebanon now carries her name. If you visit the memorial, please do so quietly, and remember a girl who should have been safe.
cases.summary: In July 1965 Lester and Betty Likens, traveling carnival concessionaires, left daughters Sylvia (16) and Jenny (15) as paying boarders with Gertrude Baniszewski in Indianapolis. Over roughly three months Sylvia was abused, starved and tortured in the house by Baniszewski, several of her children and neighborhood youths. Police called to the house on Oct 26, 1965 found Sylvia dead; the official cause was a subdural hematoma, with shock and extensive injuries contributing. A grand jury indicted Gertrude, Paula and John Baniszewski Jr., Coy Hubbard and Richard Hobbs. On May 19, 1966 a jury convicted Gertrude of first-degree murder (life), Paula of second-degree murder, and the three boys of manslaughter. The Indiana Supreme Court reversed Gertrude's and Paula's convictions in 1970 over venue/separate-trial rulings; Gertrude was convicted again in 1971 and Paula pleaded guilty to manslaughter. Gertrude was paroled in 1985 and died in 1990. The case is credited with Indiana's universal mandated-reporter law and a 2001 memorial in Willard Park.
cases.solvedHow: Not a whodunit: police found Sylvia dead in the house on Oct 26, 1965; her sister's statement and the physical evidence led to the arrests of the household and neighborhood youths, and a 1966 jury trial produced convictions.

cases.audioScript: You are on Lemon Road, north of Madison, Indiana. On the morning of January eleventh, 1992, two hunters stopped here and found twelve-year-old Shanda Sharer. Shanda had grown up in Kentucky and had just moved to New Albany, where she played basketball at Our Lady of Perpetual Help School. The night before, four teenage girls, aged fifteen to seventeen, came to her father's home in Jeffersonville and talked her into their car. Shanda kept begging to go home. Over the next hours they drove her into rural Jefferson County, beat her and set her on fire. That evening two of the girls went to the Jefferson County sheriff with their parents and told investigators what had happened, and the other two were arrested the next day. All four were charged as adults and pleaded guilty to avoid the death penalty. Two received sixty-year sentences. All four have since been released. The case drew international attention because of Shanda's age and the ages of the girls who killed her. Please remember Shanda as a twelve-year-old who loved her teams, and stay on the public road.
cases.summary: On the night of Jan 10, 1992, Melinda Loveless (16-17), Laurie Tackett (17), Hope Rippey (15) and Toni Lawrence (15) went to the Jeffersonville home of Shanda Sharer's father and lured 12-year-old Shanda into Tackett's car. According to court testimony reported by the Madison Courier, Loveless was jealous of Shanda's relationship with Loveless' former girlfriend. The girls bound, beat and stabbed Shanda over several hours, then drove north of Madison to Lemon Road off U.S. 421 in Shelby Township, Jefferson County, where they set her on fire. Hunters found her the morning of Jan 11. That evening Lawrence and Rippey gave statements at the Jefferson County Sheriff's office; Loveless and Tackett were arrested Jan 12, and Shanda was identified through dental records. All four were charged as adults and took plea bargains to avoid the death penalty. Loveless and Tackett received 60 years; Rippey ultimately 35 years; Lawrence 20 years. Lawrence, Rippey, Tackett (Jan 11, 2018) and Loveless (2019) have all been released.
cases.solvedHow: Solved within about 36 hours: two of the four girls went to the Jefferson County Sheriff with their parents and described the crime; their statements supported arrest warrants for the other two, and dental records confirmed the victim's identity.

cases.audioScript: This pin sits in Crothersville, a small town in Jackson County. On January twenty-fifth, 2005, ten-year-old Katie Collman, a fourth-grader, disappeared here. For five days the town searched. On January thirtieth her body was found in a creek about fifteen miles from home. The case drew national attention when another man came forward with a story tying her death to a methamphetamine operation. Prosecutors spent about nine weeks checking that story and found no corroboration. In May 2005 they dismissed those charges and said the confession was false. Investigators had a different lead: DNA from a cigarette found near where Katie was recovered. It matched Anthony Stockelman, a former factory worker who had been helping his mother move that day. Investigators also matched red carpet fibers on Katie's clothing to his mother's home. In March 2006 Stockelman pleaded guilty to murder and child molesting so the state would drop the death penalty, and he was sentenced to life in prison. Katie's father said there would never be closure, only a little satisfaction. Remember Katie, and the community that searched for her.
cases.summary: Katie Collman, 10, of Crothersville was abducted on Jan 25, 2005. After a five-day search her body was found Jan 30, 2005 in a creek about 15 miles from her home. A man who gave a confession was initially charged with murder, claiming she had stumbled on a meth operation; after nine weeks of failed corroboration, Jackson County Prosecutor Stephen Pierson called the story false and dismissed those charges in May 2005. DNA recovered from a cigarette butt near the scene matched Anthony Ray Stockelman, who was arrested on a molestation charge April 6, 2005 and later charged with murder. Fourteen red carpet fibers on Katie's clothing matched carpet at his mother's home. On Mar 24, 2006, in exchange for the state dropping the death penalty, Stockelman pleaded guilty to murder and child molesting before Judge William Vance in Brownstown; in April 2006 he was sentenced to life in prison plus 30 years.
cases.solvedHow: DNA from a cigarette butt near the recovery site, plus trace (carpet fiber) evidence, identified Stockelman after a false confession had diverted investigators for about nine weeks.

cases.audioScript: This pin is at Indiana University's Student Recreational Sports Center in Bloomington. On the morning of May thirty-first, 2000, nineteen-year-old Jill Behrman, an IU student, cyclist and Rec Sports employee, set out on a bike ride and never came back. For almost three years her family and friends searched Monroe and Morgan counties and far beyond. On March tenth, 2003, hunters found her remains in Morgan County. She had been shot. The Indiana State Police led the investigation, with Bloomington police and the FBI. In October 2006 a jury convicted John Myers the second of her murder, and he was sentenced to sixty-five years, the maximum. In 2019 a federal judge threw out the verdict, finding his trial lawyer had been ineffective. In August 2020 the federal appeals court reinstated the conviction, saying the evidence was strong enough to convict anyway. Every fall, IU Recreational Sports hosts the Jill Behrman 5K, a color run that raises money for a scholarship in her name. Her mother says Jill would have loved it. Remember a young woman who loved to ride.
cases.summary: Jill Behrman, 19, an IU student and employee of the Student Recreational Sports Center, disappeared during a bicycle ride from her Bloomington home on May 31, 2000. Her family and friends spent years searching. On Mar 10, 2003 hunters found her remains in Morgan County; she died of a shotgun wound to the back of the head. The Indiana State Police led the investigation with Bloomington PD and the FBI. After a grand jury investigation, John R. Myers II of Ellettsville was convicted of murder on Oct 30, 2006 and sentenced Dec 1, 2006 to 65 years, the maximum. In 2019 U.S. District Judge James Sweeney granted habeas relief, finding Myers' trial counsel ineffective; on Aug 4, 2020 the 7th Circuit (Myers v. Neal, No. 19-3158) reversed, finding counsel deficient but not prejudicial given the State's evidence, especially Myers' self-incriminating statements. On remand Judge Sweeney denied habeas relief again. Myers remains in prison.
cases.solvedHow: After her remains were found in 2003, an Indiana State Police-led investigation and a grand jury led to Myers' 2006 conviction; the 7th Circuit relied on his numerous self-incriminating statements to uphold it.

cases.audioScript: You're at Indiana State University in Terre Haute. On the night of September fifteenth, 1972, nineteen-year-old Pam Milam left a sorority event on this campus. When she didn't come home, her father went looking, and the next night he and her sister found her in the trunk of her own car. She had been bound and killed. For decades police believed a man arrested weeks later for attacks on campus was responsible, but DNA testing in 2001 ruled him out. In 2008 Terre Haute's assistant chief of investigations, Shawn Keen, took the case on himself. By 2018 only a sliver of the original DNA sample was left. He gambled it on a new technique, genetic genealogy, working with Parabon NanoLabs. The family tree led to Jeffrey Lynn Hand, a man from southern Indiana who had been killed in a police shootout in Kokomo in 1978. Hand's sons gave DNA, and the match was ninety-nine point nine percent. In May 2019 police announced the case solved. Hand was identified by police, but never charged or convicted, because he had died. Keen said calling Pam's family was the best call he ever made.
cases.summary: Pamela Milam, 19, an Indiana State University student, was last seen leaving a sorority event on the night of Sept 15, 1972. Her father (with her sister, per Fox News) found her bound and gagged in the trunk of her car; she had been strangled. Sources differ on whether she was sexually assaulted (Fox News says raped; Wikipedia's Hand article says no signs) and on the discovery date (Sept 16 per NBC/Fox; Sept 15 per Wikipedia). A man arrested about seven weeks later for campus sexual assaults was long suspected but was excluded by DNA in 2001. Shawn Keen took over the case in 2008; touch DNA on the ropes indicated a single offender. In 2018, with little sample left, Keen worked with Parabon NanoLabs; a GEDmatch upload led to relatives in Washington and Odon, Indiana (spelled 'Oden' by 14 News) and then to Jeffrey Lynn Hand (1949-1978). Hand had been found not guilty by reason of insanity in a 1973 hitchhiker killing and was shot dead by Kokomo police in January 1978 during an attempted abduction. DNA from Hand's sons gave a 99.9% probability match. On May 6, 2019 THPD announced the case solved; the prosecutor found probable cause for an arrest warrant had Hand been alive. Hand was identified by police, never charged/convicted.
cases.solvedHow: Forensic genetic genealogy (GEDmatch upload via Parabon NanoLabs) narrowed the suspect to Jeffrey Lynn Hand's family; DNA from his sons confirmed the match. Because Hand died in 1978, he was identified by police, never charged/convicted.

cases.audioScript: This pin marks the small town of Dale in Spencer County. On July eleventh, 2001, fifteen-year-old Stacy Payne was home on summer break, getting ready for her job at a pizza place. Stacy was about to start her sophomore year at Heritage Hills High School. She was an honor student and a cheerleader, she served on student council, and she played flute in the marching band. That afternoon a man named Roy Lee Ward came to the door claiming he was looking for a lost dog. He forced his way in and attacked her. Her younger sister hid and called for help, and Dale's town marshal arrived within minutes and arrested Ward at the door. Stacy was flown to a hospital in Louisville but did not survive. Ward was convicted in 2002. That verdict was overturned over pretrial publicity, and a jury from Clay County convicted him again in 2007. After her death, Stacy's family pushed for tougher sentences for repeat offenders, because Ward had a long record. Ward was executed in October 2025. Her mother says Stacy should be remembered for the life she lived.
cases.summary: On July 11, 2001, Roy Lee Ward came to the Payne home in Dale, claiming to look for a missing dog, forced his way in, and raped and stabbed 15-year-old Stacy Payne. Her sister hid and called police; Dale Town Marshal Matt Keller arrived within minutes and arrested Ward. Stacy was airlifted to University of Louisville Hospital, where she died. Ward was charged July 16, 2001, convicted by a Spencer County jury Oct 18, 2002 and sentenced to death Dec 18, 2002. After decades of appeals, Ward (53) was executed by lethal injection at Indiana State Prison and pronounced dead at 12:33 a.m. CDT on Oct 10, 2025. Stacy's family advocated for longer sentences for repeat public-indecency offenders because Ward had many prior convictions.

cases.audioScript: This pin marks the Allen County Courthouse in downtown Fort Wayne. On July twenty-sixth, 1997, four men were together in a house on the city's north side, watching television: James Corcoran, who was thirty; his sister's fiancé, Robert Scott Turner, thirty-two; and their friends Timothy Bricker and Douglas Stillwell, both thirty. Upstairs was James's twenty-two-year-old brother, Joseph. Joseph Corcoran later told police he believed the men were talking about him. He first put his seven-year-old niece in an upstairs bedroom, then came down with a rifle and killed all four men. Afterward he laid the rifle down, walked to a neighbor's house and asked them to call the police. In 1999 a unanimous jury convicted him of four counts of murder, and he was sentenced to death. His lawyers argued for decades that serious mental illness should spare him. In the early hours of December eighteenth, 2024, Joseph Corcoran became the first person Indiana had executed since 2009. Here, remember the four men, a brother, a fiancé and two friends, who were simply spending a summer evening together.
cases.summary: On July 26, 1997, Joseph Corcoran, 22, shot and killed his brother James Corcoran (30), his sister's fiancé Robert Scott Turner (32), and friends Timothy G. Bricker (30) and Douglas A. Stillwell (30) at the Fort Wayne home he shared with his brother and sister. He told police the men had been talking about him. He first placed his 7-year-old niece in an upstairs bedroom, then fired, laid down the rifle, went to a neighbor's house and asked them to call police. Over 30 firearms, munitions and explosives were found in his room and attic. In 1999 a unanimous jury found him guilty of four counts of murder; Allen Superior Court Judge Frances Gull sentenced him to death on Aug 26, 1999. The sentence went through years of appeals - including a 2000 Indiana Supreme Court remand for resentencing and a 2007 federal vacatur later reversed - amid arguments that he had paranoid schizophrenia. Corcoran was executed by lethal injection at Indiana State Prison, pronounced dead at 12:44 a.m. on Dec 18, 2024, Indiana's first execution since 2009. As a juvenile he had been charged with killing his parents in 1992 and was acquitted.
cases.solvedHow: No mystery: Corcoran went to a neighbor and asked them to call police, and he was arrested at the scene; the legal fight centered on his sentence and mental competency.

cases.audioScript: This pin rests in Georgetown, a small town in Floyd County, near Louisville. On the night of September twenty-eighth, 2000, thirty-five-year-old Kim Camm and her children, seven-year-old Brad and five-year-old Jill, were shot and killed in their family's garage after coming home. Her husband, David Camm, a former Indiana State Police trooper, said he found them when he returned from playing basketball. He was soon charged with the murders, largely on blood-spatter testimony. He was convicted twice, and both verdicts were thrown out on appeal. Meanwhile a sweatshirt left at the scene, with the nickname Backbone written in the collar, carried DNA that matched Charles Boney, a man with a record of attacking women. His palm print was on the family's vehicle. In 2006 Boney was convicted of all three murders and sentenced to two hundred twenty-five years. He still says he is innocent. In 2013 a jury in Boone County acquitted David Camm, and the National Registry of Exonerations now lists his case. Through every trial, three lives stayed at the center of this case: Kim, Brad and Jill. Please remember them here.
cases.summary: On Sept 28, 2000, Kim Camm (35) and her children Bradley (7) and Jill (5) were shot to death in the garage of their Georgetown, Indiana home. Her husband David Camm, a former Indiana State Police trooper, said he found them after playing basketball and was soon charged, largely on blood-spatter testimony. He was convicted in March 2002; the Indiana Court of Appeals reversed in August 2004. A sweatshirt found beside Bradley bore unidentified DNA and the name 'Backbone' in the collar; in 2005 the DNA was run through a criminal database and matched Charles Boney, whose palm print was also on the SUV. Boney was convicted in January 2006 of three murders and conspiracy and sentenced Feb 23, 2006 to 225 years; he maintains he killed no one. Camm was convicted again on Mar 3, 2006; the Indiana Supreme Court reversed in 2009. At a third trial in Boone County, Camm was acquitted Oct 24, 2013 and released; the National Registry of Exonerations lists his case. In August 2023 a Floyd County judge entered $1 million wrongful-death judgments against Boney for each of the three victims.
cases.solvedHow: A DNA database search on the 'Backbone' sweatshirt and a palm-print comparison identified Charles Boney in 2005, five years after the murders; he was convicted in 2006. The husband's two convictions were reversed and he was acquitted in 2013.

cases.audioScript: This pin marks a motel on 179th Street in Hammond. On October seventeenth, 2014, nineteen-year-old Afrikka Hardy was found dead in a room here. Her family said she wanted to be a doctor and was trying to get back into school. Hammond police traced the man she had met, Darren Vann, and arrested him the next day. During questioning he told detectives about other women, and he led police to abandoned houses in Gary. Over that weekend they found six more: Anith Jones, thirty-five; Teaira Batey, twenty-eight, a young mother engaged to be married; Kristine Williams, thirty-six; Tracy Martin, forty-one; Sonya Billingsley, fifty-three; and Tanya Gatlin, twenty-seven. Some had been missing for months, and for several no one had filed a missing-person report. In May 2018 Vann pleaded guilty to all seven murders in exchange for prosecutors dropping the death penalty, and he was sentenced to life without parole. At the sentencing, Lake County's prosecutor called him a prolific serial killer who touched many lives. Please speak their names: Afrikka, Anith, Teaira, Kristine, Tracy, Sonya and Tanya.
cases.summary: On Oct 17, 2014, 19-year-old Afrikka Hardy was found strangled in a bathtub at a Motel 6 on 179th Street in Hammond. Hammond police tracked Darren Vann, a Gary resident and registered sex offender in Texas, through the phone number he had used to arrange the meeting, and arrested him Oct 18. During interrogation he directed police to abandoned houses in Gary, where six more women were found Oct 18-19: Anith Jones (35), Teaira Batey (28), Kristine Williams (36), Tracy Martin (41), Sonya Billingsley (53) and Tanya Gatlin (27). Police said several had no missing-person reports. On May 4, 2018 Vann pleaded guilty to seven murders in exchange for prosecutors dropping the death penalty, and on May 25, 2018 Lake Superior Court Judge Samuel Cappas sentenced him to seven concurrent life sentences without parole.

cases.audioScript: This pin sits in Hammond, in Lake County. On June twenty-fifth, 1999, seventy-four-year-old Marion Lowry, who owned a business called Calumet Auto Rebuilders, and sixty-seven-year-old Harvey Siegers, who worked for him, were attacked inside the shop with a hammer. Mr. Lowry died there, and Mr. Siegers died later at the hospital. The shop sat in territory claimed by the Latin Kings street gang. According to the federal appeals court, gang members believed the two men were talking to police, and they had already smashed car windows at the shop to frighten them. A neighbor saw a man running away, and within hours she worked with an ATF agent to build a composite sketch that people in the community recognized. Still, the case sat unsolved for almost twenty years. It was finally brought into a sweeping federal racketeering prosecution of the Latin Kings. In July 2019 a federal jury in Hammond convicted gang member Jeremiah Farmer and found that he had committed both murders. He was sentenced to life in prison, and the appeals court upheld it in 2022. Remember two men who were simply at work.
cases.summary: On June 25, 1999, Marion Lowry (74), owner of Calumet Auto Rebuilders in Hammond, and employee Harvey Siegers (67) were beaten with a hammer at the business. Lowry died at the scene; Siegers died later at the hospital. According to the 7th Circuit, the shop sat in Latin Kings territory and members, including Farmer, believed the men were 'snitching' to police. A witness who saw a man fleeing worked with an ATF agent the same day on a composite sketch, which acquaintances said resembled Farmer; later witnesses testified that he repeatedly admitted the killings, and his sunglasses were recovered at the scene. Hammond police showed the eyewitness a photo array in 2001 (no positive identification) and executed a search warrant. Farmer was eventually charged in a federal racketeering case against the Latin Kings (Fifth Superseding Indictment, Oct 18, 2018). A jury in the Northern District of Indiana (Judge Philip Simon) convicted him on July 9, 2019, with a special finding that he murdered Lowry and Siegers; he received a mandatory life sentence, and the 7th Circuit affirmed on June 28, 2022.
cases.solvedHow: Solved as part of a federal racketeering prosecution of the Latin Kings: cooperating witnesses' testimony about Farmer's admissions, sunglasses found at the scene, and a 1999 composite sketch supported a jury special finding two decades later.

cases.audioScript: This pin marks the Indianapolis City-County Building, where the case for Amanda Blackburn was finally closed. Amanda was twenty-eight. She and her husband Davey had moved from South Carolina in 2012 to start a church here, called Resonate. She was the mother of a little boy and was about twelve weeks pregnant. Early on the morning of November tenth, 2015, three men who had been burglarizing homes broke into the Blackburns' home. They forced Amanda to go with them to an ATM, then brought her back, and she was shot. She died two days later. Investigators found DNA on a stolen sweater, studied ATM photos, and tracked a phone, and within about two weeks all three were arrested. The prosecutor called the DNA a big break. Years of court proceedings followed. Two of the men pleaded guilty to robbery and burglary. In 2022 the third, Larry Jo Taylor Junior, was convicted of her murder and sentenced to eighty-six years, and the appeals court upheld it. Her family has spoken often about grace. Remember Amanda as a mother, a wife, and a builder of community.
cases.summary: Early on Nov 10, 2015, three men broke into the Indianapolis home of Amanda Blackburn, 28, wife of Resonate Church pastor Davey Blackburn and about 12 weeks pregnant. According to the Court of Appeals, they took property including a pink sweater, forced her to go to ATMs, and Larry Jo Taylor Jr. shot her; she died Nov 12. DNA on the sweater matched co-defendant Jalen Watson, ATM photos and phone records led police to the others, and Taylor was arrested Nov 22, 2015. Marion County Prosecutor Terry Curry said DNA testing was a big break. Watson and Diano Gordon later pleaded guilty to robbery and burglary (murder charges dropped) and received 29 and 25 years. Taylor was found guilty of murder in September 2022 and sentenced in October 2022 to 86 years; the Court of Appeals affirmed on Nov 9, 2023 (No. 22A-CR-2615).

cases.audioScript: This pin marks Pinhook Park in South Bend. In June 1988, twenty-eight-year-old Miriam Rice, the mother of a three-year-old son and four months pregnant, went out to walk her dog and never came home. Her dog was found the next day, hiding under a car. Five days after she vanished, searchers found her down an embankment across this park's north lagoon. For nearly thirty years the case went unsolved. Then, in 2016, a man named George Kearney, recently out of prison, went to investigators. He said he had been receiving letters asking about his role in her death. Detectives followed the trail to the children of his former girlfriend, Barbara Brewster. They had been small children, camping with the adults near this park in 1988, and as grown-ups they told investigators what they had seen and heard. Kearney pleaded guilty to murder in 2019 and died of cancer days later. A jury convicted Brewster that June, and a judge called it the worst of the worst kind of murder as he sentenced her to sixty years. Remember Miriam here: a young mother out for an evening walk.
cases.summary: In June 1988 Miriam Rice, 28, a South Bend mother of a 3-year-old who was four months pregnant, was abducted while walking her dog; the dog was found the next day under a car on Riverside Drive. Five days later searchers found her body down an embankment on Boland Drive across Pinhook Park's north lagoon; she died of multiple skull fractures. The case was unsolved for about three decades until March 2016, when George Kearney, recently released after a long prison term for an unrelated crime, spoke with investigators after receiving letters questioning his involvement. Testimony from Barbara Brewster's children - 6 and 7 at the time, who had been at a makeshift campsite near Pinhook Park with Kearney and Brewster - described Kearney abducting Rice into a van and Brewster beating her. Kearney pleaded guilty to murder in March 2019 and died of cancer at 77 before sentencing; the court later entered a judgment of conviction. A jury convicted Brewster, 56, in June 2019, and St. Joseph County Judge John Marnocha sentenced her to 60 years; she maintained her innocence.
cases.solvedHow: A cold-case break: in 2016 one of the men involved came forward, and investigators then obtained eyewitness testimony from two adults who had been young children at the scene in 1988.

cases.audioScript: This pin marks the Boone County Courthouse in Lebanon. In March 2022, Nikki Wilhoite, a Boone County mother, was finishing chemotherapy for cancer. On Monday, March twenty-first, she gave her husband, Andrew, legal separation papers. Late on the night of Thursday the twenty-fourth, at their family farm outside Lebanon, he struck her in the head with a heavy cement flowerpot. He then put her in the bed of his pickup, drove to a bridge, and pushed her into a creek. The next morning, when Nikki did not show up for work, her coworkers called nine-one-one. For hours, the appeals court later wrote, her husband misdirected the search. He was charged with murder. In April 2024 a jury in this courthouse could not agree on murder but found that he acted in sudden heat, and convicted him of voluntary manslaughter. The judge gave him the maximum, thirty years, and in 2025 the Court of Appeals upheld that sentence. Nikki's family and coworkers remember a woman who kept going to work through cancer treatment. If you stop here, take a moment for her, and for everyone living with domestic violence.
cases.summary: On Monday, March 21, 2022, Nikki Wilhoite gave her husband Andrew legal separation documents (WISH describes it as filing for divorce). On the night of Thursday, March 24, at their farm in rural Boone County, he struck her in the head with a heavy cement flowerpot, placed her in the bed of his pickup truck, drove to a bridge and put her into a creek. She died of blunt force trauma to the head. When she failed to arrive at work the next morning, her coworkers called 911; according to the Court of Appeals, Wilhoite misdirected searchers for several hours before admitting what happened in an interview with Boone County Det. Adam Buell. Charged with murder, he was convicted in April 2024 of voluntary manslaughter after jurors deliberated about nine hours (Boone Superior Court I, Judge Matthew Kincaid). On June 4, 2024 he received the maximum 30 years. The Indiana Court of Appeals affirmed the sentence on July 9, 2025.

cases.audioScript: This pin marks Sellersburg, in Clark County. Lizzie Bennett Lewis was a nurse and a mother of two girls. Her husband, Mac Lewis, depended on dialysis three times a week, and Lizzie was the one who did his treatments at home. In April 2022 she told him she wanted a divorce. Inside their home, he shot her four times. Her eleven-year-old daughter and the girl's ten-year-old friend were in the house, and one bullet barely missed her daughter. It was that eleven-year-old who called nine-one-one. Police found Mac Lewis driving on State Road Sixty and arrested him without incident. At trial in October 2023, the prosecutor told jurors that when someone injures you four different times, it is not an accident, and the jury convicted Lewis of murder, attempted murder and criminal recklessness. In November the judge sentenced him to one hundred years, exactly what the state asked for. In court her daughters, by then teenagers, spoke about their mother, and her father called the verdict the first day of justice for his daughter. Remember Lizzie as a nurse who cared for people, right up to the end.
cases.summary: In April 2022, after Lizzie Bennett Lewis asked for a divorce, her husband Mac Lewis shot her four times in their Sellersburg home; she was found in a closet. Her 11-year-old daughter and a 10-year-old friend were inside; one shot barely missed her daughter, who called 911. Police found Lewis on State Road 60 and arrested him without incident. Lizzie was a nurse who performed his home dialysis. On Oct 3, 2023 a Clark County jury convicted Lewis of murder, attempted murder and criminal recklessness; on Nov 2, 2023 Clark Circuit Court 1 Judge Nick Karaffa sentenced him to 100 years, matching what Prosecutor Jeremy Mull sought.

cases.audioScript: This pin marks the Delaware County Building in downtown Muncie. Monica Brown was thirty-five, a mother of four. In the early morning hours of Christmas Eve, 2009, two men went to her home intending to steal her purse and her prescription pain medication. Monica was stabbed many times and killed. She was found two days later, on December twenty-sixth. For about a year and a half there were no charges. Then, in 2011, a person close to one of the men anonymously called Muncie police and said who was responsible. That tip led detectives to other people with information. In 2014 the second man gave a statement and was arrested, and in March 2015 prosecutors charged Danny Saintignon Junior with Monica's murder. The co-defendant testified against him at trial. In October 2017, after a two-week trial, a jury found Saintignon guilty of murder, robbery and conspiracy, and he was sentenced to more than one hundred thirty-seven years. The Court of Appeals upheld the conviction in 2019. Christmas Eve is a hard anniversary for her family. If you're here, remember Monica, and her four children.
cases.summary: Early on Dec 24, 2009, Monica Brown, 35, a Muncie mother of four, was attacked in her home during a robbery aimed at her purse and prescription pain medication; prosecutors said she was stabbed as many as 70 times. Muncie police found her on Dec 26, 2009. The case went cold until 2011, when an anonymous tip named Danny Saintignon Jr.; a co-defendant gave a statement and was arrested in March 2014, and on March 30, 2015 the State charged Saintignon. The co-defendant testified at trial (Sept 25-Oct 10, 2017), and the jury found Saintignon guilty as charged. At a January 2018 sentencing he received an aggregate 137 1/2 years. The Indiana Court of Appeals (Judge Patricia Riley) affirmed on Jan 17, 2019.

cases.audioScript: This pin rests in Mooresville, in Morgan County. On Saturday morning, April twenty-eighth, 1979, Terry Lee Chasteen was driving her three young children to a babysitter before work: Misty, who was five, Steve, who was four, and Mark, who was two. A man on the road signaled that something was wrong with her tire. He pretended to help, disabled her car, and offered the family a ride. He drove them to White Lick Creek. There he attacked and killed Terry, and drowned all three children. That same day police found the family. The man was Steven Judy, twenty-two, who was already out on bond for an earlier violent crime. He confessed. In February 1980 a Morgan County jury convicted him of four murders, and he asked for, and received, a death sentence. He refused to appeal, and on March ninth, 1981, he was executed in the electric chair at Indiana State Prison, the state's first execution in about twenty years. His case shaped Indiana's death-penalty debate for decades. But here, remember a mother and three small children who were simply on their way to start the day.
cases.summary: On April 28, 1979, Steven T. Judy, then 22 and free on bond for a 1977 robbery, signaled to Terry Lee Chasteen that her car had a tire problem, disabled the car while pretending to help, and offered her and her three children - Misty (5), Steve (4) and Mark (2) - a ride. He drove them to White Lick Creek in Morgan County, where he raped and strangled Terry and drowned the three children. The bodies were found that day. Judy confessed but pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity. A Morgan County jury convicted him on Feb 2, 1980 of four murders, and he was sentenced to death on Feb 25, 1980 after telling the court he would kill again. He refused to appeal and was executed in the electric chair at Indiana State Prison on March 9, 1981, aged 24 - Indiana's first execution in about two decades and the fourth in the U.S. after capital punishment was reinstated in 1976.

cases.audioScript: This pin marks Irvington, the east-side Indianapolis neighborhood where Madge Oberholtzer grew up. Madge was born in Clay City in 1896, studied at Butler University here in Irvington, and by 1924 managed a state reading program for young people. In March 1925 she was taken by D. C. Stephenson, the Grand Dragon of the Ku Klux Klan in Indiana, one of the most powerful men in the state. His men forced her onto a train toward Chicago, and he assaulted her on the way. At a hotel in Hammond, desperate, she swallowed mercury tablets. Stephenson refused to get her proper medical care and brought her back to Indianapolis. Before she died on April fourteenth, 1925, Madge gave a sworn dying declaration describing what he had done. That statement was read to the jury at his trial in Noblesville, and in November 1925 Stephenson was convicted of second-degree murder and sentenced to life. His fall, and the scandal around it, helped break the Klan's grip on Indiana politics. Madge never saw the trial. But her own words, given in her final days, are why it happened. Remember her courage here.
cases.summary: Madge Oberholtzer (born Nov 10, 1896, Clay City) grew up in Irvington, attended Butler University's Irvington campus, and in 1924 managed the Young People's Reading Circle at the Indiana State House. In March 1925 Klan Grand Dragon D.C. Stephenson had her brought to his Irvington home and forced onto a train to Chicago, assaulting her on the way. The party got off at Hammond and held her at the Indiana Hotel, where she swallowed mercuric chloride tablets (three per Wikipedia; six per Encyclopedia of Indianapolis). Stephenson refused to get her to a hospital and returned her to Indianapolis. On March 28, 1925 she gave a dying declaration to attorney Asa J. Smith; she died April 14, 1925. With a change of venue to Noblesville, a Hamilton County jury found Stephenson guilty of second-degree murder on Nov 14, 1925, and he was sentenced to life. He was paroled in 1950 and died in 1966. The verdict is credited with hastening the Klan's collapse in Indiana.
cases.solvedHow: Madge's sworn dying declaration, taken by an attorney before her death, became the core of the prosecution.

cases.audioScript: Becky Maners was sixty-two years old, a grandmother from Clayton, Indiana, and a familiar face at community events in Hendricks County. For years she served on the board of Mental Health America of Hendricks County, and the group says she raised more than fifty thousand dollars for mental wellness and suicide prevention. On Friday, July fourteenth, 2023, Becky was found dead inside a home near the small community of Belleville. Investigators ruled her death a homicide. Ten days later, the Hendricks County Sheriff's Office asked for help finding one specific person: the driver of a white, full-sized pickup truck who gave someone a ride heading west through Belleville that same day. Detectives said the driver, or the passenger, may have seen something important. In February 2024 the sheriff's office said forensic work would continue as technology improves, with help from the FBI and Indiana State Police. No arrest has been announced. If you drove that truck, or know who did, please call Detective Sergeant Sam Chandler.

cases.audioScript: Candace Powell was thirty-one, a mother of four from Indianapolis, and her mom says her smile could brighten any room. Just after two in the morning on March fourteenth, 2024, Candace was at a Marathon gas station on Prospect Street in the Fountain Square neighborhood. Police say surveillance video shows an argument, and a witness told investigators her boyfriend shot her in her car. Someone drove Candace to IU Health Methodist Hospital in her own vehicle, where she died. Prosecutors charged that boyfriend, thirty-four-year-old Deandre Rogers, with murder and two gun crimes, including possessing a firearm as a domestic batterer. But Rogers has never been found. Police say he has ties to Atlanta and Houston and should be considered armed and dangerous. Candace's four children are now being raised by her mother, who is urging anyone in an abusive relationship to speak up and get help. If you know where Deandre Rogers is, call 911 or Crime Stoppers of Central Indiana. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

Charges of murder and two firearm counts were filed under seal on Mar 25, 2024 and unsealed in late May 2024, when IMPD asked for help locating Rogers, 34, who has ties to Houston and Atlanta. As of Solve the Case's May 2026 update he remained at large. Charges are allegations; he has not been tried.

cases.audioScript: Hayden Manis has blue eyes, brown hair, and a family who wishes they had known sooner. Hayden was born in May 2015. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children lists him as last seen on January eleventh, 2020, in Muncie, Indiana, when he was just four years old. Incredibly, no one reported him missing until late 2024, more than four years later. Relatives say they believed he was being cared for elsewhere, and only then realized none of them had seen him in years. The Delaware County Sheriff's Office opened an investigation, searched properties, and in February 2025 Muncie Crime Stoppers offered a one-thousand-dollar reward for information leading to Hayden. The county prosecutor has called the case one that haunts him. In May 2026, on what would have been Hayden's eleventh birthday, he said he was leaning toward filing criminal charges, but none have been filed. NCMEC has released an image showing how Hayden might look today. If you know anything, contact the Delaware County Sheriff's Office or call 1-800-THE-LOST.

cases.audioScript: Cristina Pina was forty-nine years old and lived on a quiet street in Elkhart, Indiana. cases.audioScript: In the dark, early hours of November ninth, 2017, three women arrived at a home on Sherwood Terrace, on the south side of Fort Wayne, Indiana. At about five minutes after four in the morning, someone found all three lying in front of the house, shot. When officers arrived, one woman was already dead. Another died at the hospital. cases.audioScript: Joey Ross was twenty-five, from Brownstown, Indiana, and worked for O'Reilly Auto Parts. On Sunday, May thirteenth, 2018, a friend brought him to a home in the Amberley Addition, just south of Columbus. Between seven and seven thirty that evening, Joey walked down the driveway and into the dark. The Bartholomew County Sheriff's Department later said he was reported to be in crisis and carrying a shotgun. A search began that night, but Joey could not be found. His father reported him missing the next day. People in the area reported hearing gunshots, but over the following week searchers found no shotgun, no shells, and no sign of Joey at all. More than four years later, in November 2022, the sheriff's department renewed its call for tips. Joey is five foot six, about one hundred thirty-five pounds, with blond hair and hazel eyes. He is still listed on Indiana's missing person bulletin. If you have any information about Joey Ross, please contact the Bartholomew County Sheriff's Department. His family is still looking for him.
