cases.audioScript: On July twenty-fifth, 2015, twenty-one-year-old Diamond Bynum and her two-year-old nephew, King Walker, were last seen at a family home in Gary, Indiana. Their family believes Diamond took King for a walk, and they never came back. Diamond has Prader-Willi syndrome, a genetic condition, and her family says she has the understanding of a young child. She needs daily medication. The family had moved to Gary from Hammond only months earlier, and she did not know the neighborhood well. Because King was with an adult, no Amber Alert was issued, and it took about six weeks for a Silver Alert to go out. There were reported sightings, but none led to the pair. Her father has said he believes someone may be keeping Diamond from contacting him. Every year since, the family has gathered to plead for help. King would now be a teenager, and the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children has released an image of how he might look. Both are still listed as missing in Indiana. If you have seen Diamond or King, call the Gary Police Department or 1-800-THE-LOST.
cases.summary: Diamond Bynum, 21, who has Prader-Willi syndrome and the mental capacity of a young child, and her 2-year-old nephew King Walker disappeared from Gary on July 25, 2015 after going for a walk near their home. NCMEC lists King as possibly in Diamond's company and has released age progressions. As of 2026 both remain on the Indiana State Police missing person bulletin and the family continues annual appeals.

cases.audioScript: Desta Clark was twenty years old, and his friends called him a sweet guy and always a great friend. Just before six in the morning on May twenty-fifth, 2022, people near apartments on South Clarizz Boulevard in Bloomington, Indiana, called nine-one-one to report several gunshots. Officers could not find a victim at first. They did find an apartment with a back door that had been forced open, but no one was inside. For more than an hour, officers searched, until they checked a heavily wooded area west of the buildings. There, at about seven twenty, an officer found Desta. He had been shot multiple times. Investigators later learned from the apartment's resident that two men in face coverings had kicked in the door and chased Desta out just before the shooting. No other suspect information has been released, and no arrests have been announced. His mother has pleaded for answers. If you know anything about the morning of May twenty-fifth, please call Bloomington Police Detective Wade Berry.
cases.summary: At about 5:55 a.m. on May 25, 2022, Bloomington police responded to the 700 block of South Clarizz Boulevard for multiple 911 calls about shots fired. They found an apartment whose rear door appeared forced but was empty, and after more than an hour found Desta Clark, 20, dead of multiple gunshot wounds in a heavily wooded area west of the apartments. The apartment's resident told police two men in face coverings kicked in the door and chased the victim out shortly before the shooting. No further suspect information has been released; Herald-Times coverage in 2022-2024 reported no arrests.

cases.audioScript: Kalin Washington was sixteen years old when she went to a Halloween party on the north side of Indianapolis in October 2023. Invitations had spread on Snapchat, and hundreds of young people showed up at a business on East Sixty-fifth Street. There was no permit for the event. Just after midnight, as police arrived to check on the party, they heard gunshots and saw a crowd running. Kalin had been shot, and she died at the scene. Nine other young people, ages sixteen to twenty-one, were wounded. Police found six guns and many shell casings. A deputy chief stood before cameras and begged anyone with information to come forward, saying no one deserves to die at sixteen because they went to a party. More than a year later, prosecutors charged a nineteen-year-old with reckless homicide and many other counts for organizing and promoting that party and others like it. He is not accused of firing the shots, and he is presumed innocent. The person or people who killed Kalin have never been charged. If you were there, please call IMPD or Crime Stoppers.
cases.summary: Around midnight Oct 29, 2023, IMPD officers responding to a large party at a business in the 5000 block of East 65th Street heard gunfire and saw a crowd fleeing. Kalin Washington, 16, was pronounced dead and nine others aged 16-21 were wounded. Six firearms and many casings were recovered. The event had no permit and had been promoted through Snapchat. On Dec 13, 2024, the Marion County Prosecutor charged Jalen Helm, 19, with 31 counts including reckless homicide for allegedly organizing, promoting and hosting illegal parties; he is not accused of being the shooter and is presumed innocent. As of WRTV's Oct 2024 anniversary report, no shooter had been charged, and none has been reported since.

cases.audioScript: Joseph Chaffins was twenty-six and lived in Pierceton, a small town in Kosciusko County, in northern Indiana's lake country. He was last seen around October twenty-sixth, 2022, on Backwater Road in North Webster. After that, his family never saw or heard from him again. In December 2022, the Kosciusko County Sheriff's Office asked the public for help finding him. Joseph is five foot eight, about one hundred forty pounds, with brown hair and blue eyes. He has distinctive tattoos: his last name, Chaffins, and a cross on his left forearm; the words Momma's Boy on the right side of his chest; and a red dog on his right hip. In January 2025, more than two years later, the sheriff's office shared his poster again, saying any information, big or small, could help. He remains on the Indiana State Police missing person bulletin. If you recognize Joseph, or know anything about where he went after October 2022, please call Kosciusko County Detective Sergeant Mike Fowler. His family is still waiting for him to come home.

cases.audioScript: On a Friday night in August 2012, seven-year-old Kristyana Jackson came home from a high school football game with her mom in Elkhart, Indiana. Her dad had stayed home with her baby brother. It was about ten thirty. Kristyana jumped out of the car to run inside and see her father. As her mother reached for her keys at the door, a group of masked, armed men came around the side of the house. Kristyana's mother screamed. Her father, John, ran to the door, and the men opened fire. John was shot three times trying to reach his daughter. Kristyana was shot in the head. She was rushed to a trauma center in South Bend, and she died two days later, on August nineteenth. Her parents say they had no enemies. Every year on that date, family and friends release purple balloons, her favorite color. In 2025, the county prosecutor called it an open and active case and said she wants it solved. Michiana Crime Stoppers offers an enhanced reward of six thousand dollars. If you know anything, please call Michiana Crime Stoppers.
cases.summary: About 10:30 p.m. Friday Aug 17, 2012, Kristyana Jackson, 7, and her mother were returning home from a football game to their home on Kilbourn Street in Elkhart, when multiple masked, armed men approached. When her father John came to the door, the men opened fire; John was shot three times and survived; Kristyana was shot in the head and died Aug 19 at Memorial Hospital in South Bend. The men fled on foot. There had been a string of neighborhood break-ins that month. No one has been charged. In Aug 2025 her parents publicly urged faster action; Prosecutor Vicki Becker said she considers it an open and active case. Michiana Crime Stoppers offers $6,000.

cases.audioScript: On the morning of October third, 1970, ten-year-old Jerry Michael Bayles, known as Mike, set out before dawn to deliver the Indianapolis Star on the city's west side. He was filling in on his older brother's paper route. Around five o'clock, after only a couple of papers had been delivered, Mike vanished near South Harris Street. His bicycle was found left behind. Within hours, a farmer found Mike's body in rural western Henry County, north of Knightstown. He had been stabbed. A man was arrested early in the investigation but was not indicted, and no one has ever been charged. In 2015, a new tip brought the case back into the news, and Indiana State Police said they were working to confirm it, but the man named in that tip has died and little physical evidence remains. More than fifty years later, the Indiana State Police Pendleton District still lists Mike's murder as an open cold case. If you know anything, even something small that you have carried for decades, investigators want to hear it. Mike was a shy, smiling boy, and his friends still remember him.

cases.audioScript: In August 1972, twenty-five-year-old Vickie Lynn Harrell was living in Bloomington, Indiana. On August twelfth, she was seen getting into her dark blue 1965 Plymouth Valiant in a K-Mart parking lot on the east side of town. The next day, her roommate reported her missing to Bloomington police. On August fourteenth, two things happened. Her car turned up in a parking lot near the College Mall, and her body was found in neighboring Owen County, on an access road to McCormick's Creek State Park, about two and a half miles east of Spencer. Indiana State Police say she had been strangled. More than fifty years later, no one has been charged, and the Indiana State Police Bloomington District still lists her case as an open cold case. Vickie's case has drawn renewed attention from podcasters and local reporters, but the key question remains: who did she meet after leaving that parking lot? If you lived in Bloomington or Owen County in the summer of 1972 and remember anything about Vickie or her blue Valiant, the Indiana State Police want to hear from you.

cases.audioScript: In October 1974, nineteen-year-old Debra Ann Wilhite was a young mother of two, working evening shifts as a server at the Windmill, a truck-stop restaurant near U.S. 41 and State Road 57 north of Evansville. Near the end of her shift on October sixteenth, a man came in, wet from the rain, asking for a ride. Debra was last seen speaking with him, and then she left in her green 1966 Ford Galaxie. Neither Debra nor her car has ever been found. Because she was not reported missing right away, precious time was lost. Over the years, investigators have followed rumors about ponds and old strip pits, and in 2025 a volunteer dive team, working with her family, used sonar to search a wildlife area in Warrick County. They found nothing there, but planned to check more waterways between Evansville and Princeton. The Indiana State Police still list Debra's disappearance as an open case. Her daughter has spent her life searching for answers. If you remember a green Ford Galaxie with Indiana plate 26B2953, please call the Indiana State Police.

cases.audioScript: On Monday morning, September twelfth, 1977, twenty-year-old Ann Harmeier left her hometown of Cambridge City, Indiana, to drive back to Indiana University in Bloomington. She was a junior and a theater major, and she had a ten-thirty class she never missed. Her rust-colored 1971 Pontiac LeMans overheated and broke down on State Road 37, about two miles north of Martinsville. That night her mother and a friend, retracing her route, found the car on the shoulder, locked, with the hazard lights flashing and her laundry and books still inside. Ann was gone. State police and the Morgan County Sheriff set up road checks and stopped drivers to ask what they had seen. Thirty-six days later, a farmer found Ann's body in a cornfield about seven miles northeast of Martinsville. She had been strangled. Evidence from the scene was preserved and has been tested for DNA, with no match so far. Today, her cousin runs a social media campaign telling the story in Ann's own voice, hoping someone finally talks. Indiana State Police say the case remains under investigation.
cases.summary: Ann Louise Harmeier, 20, an IU junior theater major from Cambridge City, set out for Bloomington on Sept 12, 1977. Her 1971 Pontiac LeMans overheated and was found on the shoulder of SR 37 about 2 miles north of Martinsville, locked with hazard lights flashing. Her mother and a friend found the car near midnight and reported her missing. ISP and the Morgan County Sheriff ran road checks. Thirty-six days later her body was found in a cornfield about 7 miles northeast of Martinsville; ISP says she was strangled with a shoelace. In 1978 police looked for a connection with the Mary Beth 'Pixie' Grismore case (per an Indianapolis Star article shown by The Deck). DNA evidence was preserved and is occasionally tested, with no match (cousin, via NBC). ISP said in 2023 the case remains under investigation.

cases.audioScript: On January fourth, 1978, twenty-year-old Bruce Moser left work early to pick up his wife, twenty-two-year-old Margaret, for an appointment in town. The high-school sweethearts lived in a mobile home on State Road 3, just north of the Wells and Blackford county line near Montpelier, with their toddler daughter, Kerri. When Bruce did not come to work for two days, his manager asked police to check on the family. Deputies found Bruce and Margaret dead. Both had been tied up and shot. Their little girl was alive, alone in the home, hungry and frightened, after about two days. Indiana State Police took over the case. Investigators later said they focused on one man, a truck driver whose route passed the Moser home, but he died before he could be questioned further, and he was never charged. DNA was collected at the scene and is still preserved, and an ISP captain said in 2021 he would not still be working the case if he did not think it could be solved. If someone ever told you they were involved, investigators want to hear from you.

ISP took over the investigation. ISP Capt. cases.audioScript: On February twenty-second, 1978, Mary Beth Grismore, known to everyone as Pixie, was supposed to start a new life. The twenty-six-year-old mother of two had just remarried and was moving from her rural home near Marshall, in Parke County, Indiana, to join her husband in Iowa. Instead, she vanished, along with her car. A mechanic in nearby Rockville later told police he saw her car that morning with a man behind the wheel. He agreed to be hypnotized to help remember, and the FBI drew a composite sketch. In early May, police in Whitehall, Ohio, near Columbus, checked on an abandoned car in a Holiday Inn parking lot. Pixie's body was in the trunk. Many of her belongings, including oil paintings she had signed 'Pixie', a wall clock and fine china, were missing and have never turned up. Her case is on the cold-case lists of both the Indiana State Police and the Ohio Attorney General. If you ever came across a painting signed 'Pixie' or remember her car in February 1978, call the Indiana State Police or the FBI.

Household items, including oil paintings signed 'PIXIE', were missing from the car. A Rockville mechanic said he saw a man driving her car that morning; a composite sketch was produced (FBI, via The Deck). In 1978 police looked for links to the Ann Harmeier case (IN-053). The case is open in both states.

cases.audioScript: In November 1988, in the small city of Brazil, Indiana, thirty-two-year-old Ricky Mustard and his sixteen-year-old stepdaughter, Tonya Pickett, were shot and killed inside their home on West Pinckley Street. Tonya had been at a Northview High School dance that night. Their bodies were found just after one in the morning on November nineteenth, when Tonya's mother came home from work. For years the case went nowhere. Then, in 2002, the Indiana State Police assigned its cold case homicide team. Their work led to a special prosecutor, and in March 2008 a grand jury returned an indictment. But a judge ruled that nearly two hundred letters, a key part of the evidence, were hearsay and could not be used. The Court of Appeals agreed, and in 2012 the charges were dismissed. No one has been convicted. Ricky's son Shane was thirteen when he lost his father and stepsister. Now in his fifties, he calls police and reporters every November so the case is not forgotten. If you know something about that night in 1988, contact the Indiana State Police.
cases.summary: Ricky Mustard, 32, and his stepdaughter Tonya Pickett, 16, were shot in the head in their home in the 100 block of W. Pinckley St., Brazil, in November 1988; the Indiana OIG report says the bodies were found at 1:20 a.m. Nov 19 by Tonya's mother returning from work. Several early investigations failed to produce enough evidence. In July 2002 the ISP Cold Case Homicide Team was assigned; its two-year investigation led to a special prosecutor, and on March 26, 2008, a grand jury indicted one person. In 2009 a Hendricks County judge excluded letters the state relied on; the Court of Appeals upheld that ruling (2011; rehearing denied 2012) and the charges were dismissed on March 23, 2012. The case remains unsolved; the family has asked ISP's Indianapolis-based cold case team to review it.

cases.audioScript: On November eleventh, 1981, fifteen-year-old Marie Bridget Patrick and a sixteen-year-old friend set out from Cincinnati, hoping to run away to Texas. They were hitchhiking, and a semi-truck driver picked them up. He told them his name was Bill. As they rolled west on Interstate 64 into southern Indiana, he began making sexual advances and threats. Near mile marker sixty-seven in Dubois County, the girls demanded to be let out. There was a struggle, and Marie was stabbed. In the chaos, Marie shoved her friend out of the door of the moving truck. Her friend survived with a minor injury. Marie could not get out. She was found dead about five miles farther down the interstate. The trucker has never been identified. Newspapers at the time described a white cab pulling a silver-gray trailer, and police even considered hypnosis to help with the description. More than forty years later, the Indiana State Police still list Marie's case as open. Somewhere, a man called Bill may have bragged about that night, or a company may remember a driver on I-64 that week.
cases.summary: On Nov 11, 1981, Marie Bridget Patrick, 15, and a 16-year-old friend were running away from Cincinnati to Texas when a truck driver who called himself only 'Bill' picked them up. On I-64 near mile marker 67 in Dubois County he made sexual advances and threats; in the struggle Marie was stabbed, and she shoved her friend out of the moving truck. The friend survived; Marie was found dead of a fractured skull about 5 miles farther down the interstate. The trucker has never been identified. Period newspaper headlines (listed by A Heavy Weight) say police sought a trucker named 'Bill' and considered hypnosis in the investigation.

cases.audioScript: On the afternoon of February twenty-fourth, 1987, ten-year-old Linda Weldy stepped off her school bus on West McClung Road in LaPorte, Indiana. The driver and other children watched her walk toward the family mailbox at the end of a long, curving gravel driveway that led to her home, hidden by trees. She never made it to the door. Linda loved fishing, riding her bike, and the TV show Mork and Mindy. Her mother was working a late factory shift and had no phone at home, so it was close to midnight before she learned her daughter was missing. Three weeks later, a farmer found Linda's body along an abandoned railroad line near Kingsbury, miles from home. She had been strangled. Over the years, LaPorte County detectives have developed persons of interest, but no one has ever been arrested. In 2014 the sheriff's office sent old and never-before-tested evidence to the Indiana State Police lab, hoping new DNA technology could finally point to her killer. If you saw anything on McClung Road that afternoon, LaPorte County detectives still want to hear from you.

On Mar 17, 1987, a farmer found her body on an abandoned Wabash Railroad right-of-way near Kingsbury (east of US 35 off CR 500 South); she had been strangled. LaPorte County detectives say persons of interest have been developed but no arrest made. In 2014 the case was reopened and previously tested and never-tested evidence was sent to the ISP lab for DNA analysis. ABC57's 2019 'Looking for Linda's Killer' series reported investigators believed new technology could bring them closer.

cases.audioScript: In the summer of 1988, Keyla Weddel was getting ready for her twelfth year of teaching at Medora Elementary School, in a farming town of fewer than seven hundred people in Jackson County, Indiana. She was thirty-three, the mother of three small children, including twins, and she also worked part time at the county courthouse in Brownstown. Keyla lived in a mobile home behind her parents' house. She was last seen on the evening of August seventeenth. The next morning, her mother found her dead in her bedroom. She had been beaten. Police found no sign of forced entry, and nothing had been stolen. The killing changed Medora. People who had never locked their doors started locking them. Over thirty years, there have been countless tips and hundreds of interviews, and several detectives have worked the case. In 2018, the assigned Indiana State Police detective said some of Keyla's clothing and household items were at the state police lab for new testing. Her brother and sister are still waiting for justice. If you know what happened in Medora that night, call the Indiana State Police Versailles post.

Chris Howell said clothing and household items were at the ISP lab for testing with newer science. The Jackson County Public Library's True Crime Club reviewed the case in 2023.

cases.audioScript: In the early morning hours of September fifth, 1988, a neighbor on Oak Grove Road in Washington, Indiana, saw a house on fire. Inside, firefighters found the body of eighteen-year-old Rebecca Harvey, a senior at Washington High School. Indiana State Police say she had been doused with gasoline and set on fire. The house belonged to her boyfriend, twenty-two-year-old Steven Hendricks. She had moved in only two weeks earlier. Steven was nowhere to be found, and he has never been seen again. He never picked up his last paycheck from the body shop where he worked, and he left his tools behind. His wallet was found inside the burned house. Indiana State Police believe Steven was also a victim of foul play, and they list both cases as open. In 2019, acting on a tip, police searched Oak Grove Cemetery for clues to what happened to him. Two families have waited more than thirty-five years. Someone in Daviess County may know where Steven is. If that's you, call the Indiana State Police Jasper post.

ISP says evidence showed she had been doused with gasoline and set ablaze; the fire was ruled arson. Hendricks was reported missing; ISP believes he is a victim of foul play. He left behind his last paycheck, his tools and his wallet. In 2019 police searched Oak Grove Cemetery on a tip. Hendricks is listed in NamUs (MP10653, per aggregator) and the Charley Project as endangered missing.

cases.audioScript: On March twenty-ninth, 1993, nineteen-year-old Tricia Reitler, a freshman at Indiana Wesleyan University in Marion, took a break from writing a paper. She walked to a nearby Marsh supermarket, bought a soda and a magazine, and started back toward her dorm. She never arrived. Days later, investigators found her shopping bag and receipt across the street from the store, and her bloodstained clothing in a field near Seybold Pool and Center School, between the store and campus. People had been playing basketball nearby that evening, but none of them has ever come forward. Tricia was from Olmsted Township, Ohio. She was on an academic scholarship and wanted to become a psychologist to help put families back together. Her parents now say their goal is simply to bring her home. In 2023, Marion police said the case is not cold, it is active, and detectives had traveled to re-interview everyone named in the file. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children has released an age-progressed image showing how Tricia might look today. If you know anything, call the Marion Police Department.
cases.summary: Tricia Lynn Reitler, 19, an IWU freshman psychology major from Olmsted Township, Ohio, walked to a Marsh Supermarket about half a mile from campus on Mar 29, 1993, bought a soda and a magazine, and never returned to Bowman Hall. Her bloodstained jeans, shirt and shoes were found in a field near Seybold Pool and Center School; WRTV reports detectives found her bag and receipt across the street from Marsh two days later. People playing basketball nearby have never been identified. A man in federal custody for another abduction signed a confession and later recanted; police said evidence was too thin to charge (WRTV, citing 1994 reporting). Marion PD said in 2023 the case is active, with detectives re-interviewing everyone named. NCMEC case 780520 includes an age progression to 49.

cases.audioScript: On November sixth, 1997, thirteen-year-old Ricky Lane Thomas Junior called his cousin from his family's home in rural Bristow, in Perry County, Indiana. They had plans to go to Tell City, and Ricky wanted McDonald's. He said he would walk the mile or so to her house. Ricky was last seen walking along Oak Ridge Road with his two young hunting-dog puppies. He never arrived. Neither Ricky nor the puppies were ever seen again. He wasn't reported to police until the next day. Investigators searched extensively but found nothing. Indiana State Police say they believe Ricky's disappearance could be the result of a criminal act, and the detective assigned to the case said publicly that he believed Ricky had met with foul play. Ricky would be in his forties today. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children has released an age-progressed image, and Ricky has small scars on both cheeks that could help identify him. If you remember a boy with two puppies on Oak Ridge Road that November afternoon, please call the Indiana State Police Jasper post.
cases.summary: Ricky Lane Thomas Jr., 13, was last seen about 1 p.m. on Nov 6, 1997, walking along Oak Ridge Road in rural Bristow, Perry County, toward his cousin's home a mile to a mile and a half away; his two puppies also vanished. He was reported missing the next day. ISP says an extensive search did not find him and his disappearance could be the result of a criminal act; ISP Det. Sgt. Steve Chambers told 14 News he believes Ricky met with foul play. NCMEC case 840241 includes an age progression to 26. No arrests have been made.

cases.audioScript: On the evening of June seventeenth, 2002, forty-six-year-old Nancy Lyons drove from her apartment in Carthage, Indiana, to nearby Rushville to pick up groceries and medicine. On her way home, she stopped at a rural intersection, County Road 700 West and 500 North in Rush County. No one knows why. A passerby found her red 1993 Nissan a few hours later. The engine was running, the trunk was open, a back tire was flat, and Nancy's belongings, including her cell phone, were still inside. Nancy was gone. Her family searched for months. In October, a farmer in Bartholomew County found human remains in his soybean field. They were Nancy's. She had died from a blow to the head. Nancy loved to sing and dance, stay up late talking, and spoil her nieces and nephews. Her sister Beverly started The Nancy Lyons Project, gathered hundreds of letters to state officials, and helped push for Molly's Law, which improved how Indiana handles missing-person cases. No one has been arrested. If you drove past that intersection that night, call the Indiana State Police.
cases.summary: Nancy Lyons, 46, of Carthage, was returning from Rushville on June 17, 2002, when she stopped at CR 700 W and CR 500 N in Rush County. Late that evening her red 1993 Nissan (Indiana plate 39A8348) was found running, unoccupied, trunk open, left rear tire flat, with her belongings inside. On Oct 2, 2002, her skeletal remains were found in a soybean field on CR 1000 E between CR 200 S and 300 S in Bartholomew County. Medical experts determined she died from a blow to the head. No suspects have been named and no arrests made. Her sister Beverly Tallent runs The Nancy Lyons Project and campaigned for Molly's Law (2007).

cases.audioScript: On October twenty-first, 2005, in the tiny LaGrange County community of Mongo, Indiana, someone came onto the rural property of Terry and Darleen Anderson and beat them both to death. Terry, fifty-nine, worked for a tree-service company and loved to hunt. He was found in his pole barn, where he had been working on a tractor. Darleen, fifty-seven, was close to retiring after thirty-five years at Kraft Foods in Kendallville. She was found on the couch, a bowl of popcorn beside her. There was no sign of forced entry. Some things were missing from the property, including money and an old firearm, but her jewelry was left behind. For twenty years, the case has haunted Mongo. Investigators have said since 2011 that they believe they know who committed the crimes, but no charges have ever been filed, and some family members question that theory. Indiana State Police and the LaGrange County Sheriff still want to hear from anyone who saw a vehicle, heard something, or was told something about that night.
cases.summary: Terry Anderson, 59 (ISP lists 60), and Darleen Anderson, 57, were beaten to death at their rural home near Mongo, LaGrange County, on Oct 21, 2005. ISP says both died of blunt force trauma to the head; Darleen was found inside the house and Terry in an outbuilding (pole barn); items were missing from the property. InkFreeNews reports no forced entry and that money and an old muzzleloader were taken while jewelry was left. Since 2011 investigators have said they believe they know who did it, but no charges have been filed (ABC57). Family members are divided on that theory.
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. Techniques reported: scene investigation, stolen-property tracing, persons-of-interest development leading investigators to a theory in 2011 without enough evidence to charge, and continuing public appeals via the LaGrange County Sheriff.

cases.audioScript: In the early morning hours of November twenty-first, 2016, fire tore through a house on East Columbia Street in Flora, a small town in Carroll County, Indiana. Inside were four sisters: Keyana Davis, eleven; Keyara Phillips, nine; Kerriele McDonald, seven; and Kionnie Welch, five. All four girls died. Their mother, Gaylin Rose, survived with injuries, and two police officers who rushed to help were also hurt. Investigators later determined the fire had been set on purpose. It was arson. Indiana State Police lead the case, with the FBI's Indianapolis office alongside them. The house was torn down in 2023, but the case was not set aside. In July 2025, state and federal agents went door to door in Flora again. And in November 2026, as the tenth anniversary approached, the FBI announced a reward of up to fifty thousand dollars. Its Indianapolis chief said plainly: this is not a cold case. The FBI says the girls' mother is a victim, not a suspect. If you saw, heard, or were told anything about that night, call 1-800-CALL-FBI, or the Indiana State Police.
cases.summary: Early on Nov 21, 2016, a fire at 103 E. Columbia St., Flora, killed sisters Keyana Davis (11), Keyara Phillips (9), Kerriele McDonald (7) and Kionnie Welch (5). Their mother, Gaylin Rose, and two responding officers suffered non-life-threatening injuries. The fire was determined to have been intentionally set (criminal case opened Feb 2017, per Carroll County Comet). ISP leads, assisted by the Carroll County Sheriff, Flora PD and IDHS fire investigators; the FBI joined later. The house was demolished in Oct 2023. In July 2025 ISP and FBI re-canvassed the community. In Nov 2026 the FBI announced a reward of up to $50,000; ISP's reward of up to $5,000 remains. FBI SAC Tim O'Malley said it is 'not a cold case' and that the mother is a victim. A 2020 court case concerned release of 911 recordings.
cases.solvedHow: Unsolved. Techniques reported: fire-origin investigation (IDHS), joint ISP-FBI investigation, community re-canvass (2025), rewards (ISP $5,000; FBI $50,000), and media appeals; investigators say witness accounts continue to fill gaps.

cases.audioScript: On June twelfth, 1994, twenty-year-old Delmar Wilson of Paoli, Indiana, dropped his girlfriend off near Hardinsburg, in Washington County, around one in the morning. She was the last person known to have seen him alive. Later that morning, at about 7:50, a passerby found Delmar in his white 1987 Chrysler, parked on Radcliff Road about eight-tenths of a mile south of U.S. 150. He was sitting in the driver's seat. He had been shot at close range in the head. Indiana State Police have described the killing as a murder or an execution. In 2005, a state police sergeant said detectives believed Delmar knew, or thought he knew, the person or people who attacked him. The motive has never been made public. No one has been charged. The case remains on the Indiana State Police cold-case list under the Sellersburg District, case number 45-29329. Police still ask anyone with information to call the Sellersburg post at 812-246-5424, or the state police tip line. Delmar was a young man from Paoli, just across the county line in Orange County. If you were on that road that morning, or if someone later told you something about that night, please call.
cases.summary: On June 12, 1994, Delmar Wilson, 20, of Paoli, Orange County, was found shot to death in Washington County near Hardinsburg. Indiana State Police say that at about 1:00 a.m. he dropped his girlfriend off at her residence, within two miles of the later scene, and that she was the last known person to see him alive. At about 7:50 a.m. a passerby found him in his 1987 white Chrysler, parked in the roadway on Radcliff Road about 0.8 mile south of U.S. 150, sitting in the front driver's seat. He had been shot at close range in the head. ISP has described the killing as a murder or an execution and says there are no known witnesses. The official page does not name a weapon. A 2005 News and Tribune report, quoting Sgt. Jerry Goodin, said Wilson was found with the window rolled down after a shotgun blast to the face, that he had stopped at a pull-off on Radcliff Road, that detectives believed he knew or thought he knew the attacker or attackers, and that Crime Stoppers was offering a $1,000 reward. Those 2005 details are not on the current ISP page and are stamped Not Yet Verified (single news source). The case remains on the ISP Sellersburg District cold-case list as case 45-29329; no one has been charged. The request used the spelling Delmer; official and news sources use Delmar. No second matching crime case was found. The pin is the Hardinsburg village point, not the rural road and not any residence.

cases.audioScript: On November fourth, 2022, Hobart, Indiana, police went to an apartment for a well-being check. Inside, they found twenty-year-old Destiny Jackson and her partner, nineteen-year-old Nazirah Muhammad. Both young women had been shot multiple times. Investigators said they had been shot the morning before, and police later said the couple was killed in their sleep. For more than three years, the case went unsolved. Hobart police pleaded with the public for help, and Destiny's family kept her name in front of the community. Her sisters said that, thanks to the lead investigator, Corporal Michael Gallagher, they never felt the case went cold. In February 2026, Hobart police announced that two men from Gary, Amos Daylon Crim, twenty-six, and Sa Quan Dajon Kirksey, twenty-five, had been arrested and charged with two counts of murder, along with burglary counts. Both men are presumed innocent, and the case is pending in court. One of Destiny's sisters called the charges a step forward, saying Destiny was loved, she was brave, and she did not deserve what happened to her. Anyone with information is still asked to contact the Hobart Police Department.

Police later said the couple was killed in their sleep (ABC7). In February 2026, Hobart police announced the arrests of Amos Daylon Crim, 26, and Sa Quan Dajon Kirksey, 25, both of Gary, who were charged with two counts of murder and additional burglary counts (CBS Chicago; ABC7 Chicago). cases.audioScript: On the night of August eighth, 2011, twenty-six-year-old Jessica Starr arrived home in the 28000 block of Melody Lane in Elkhart County, Indiana, where she was staying with a friend. It was around eleven-thirty. She had possibly been to the grocery store, and she was unloading her car. Someone was waiting. Jessica was beaten and stabbed and left to die in the backyard. Investigators believe she was targeted and knew her attacker. The light bulb on the front porch had been unscrewed, and police think the killer waited in the dark. Jessica was three months away from her twenty-seventh birthday. Her brother Frank has called her a spitfire who was absolutely full of life. For more than a decade the case has gone unsolved. In 2023, detectives told WNDU they had a person, or persons, of interest, but needed more to make an arrest. No one has been charged, and no one is named here. Michiana Crime Stoppers offers a reward of up to twenty-five hundred dollars for a tip that solves the case. If you know what happened on Melody Lane that night, please call Crime Stoppers.

cases.audioScript: On Sunday, July twenty-second, 2001, twenty-eight-year-old Marilyn McCown, known to everyone as Niqui, spent the afternoon doing laundry in Richmond, Indiana. She was a mother, an accounting clerk at a correctional facility in Dayton, Ohio, and just weeks away from her wedding. That afternoon she told her mother that men at the laundromat had been bothering her. Then she left, and she never came home. About four months later, police found the GMC Jimmy she had been driving at an apartment complex in Dayton. Her laundry was still inside, folded in a basket. There were no signs of a struggle. Niqui has never been found, and no one has ever been charged. Richmond police say the case is not closed. In 2026, detectives said they are going back through the evidence, including items recovered from her vehicle, to see whether newer DNA and fingerprint technology can tell them something it couldn't twenty years ago. Her family still holds a candlelight vigil every July near the spot where she was last seen. If you know anything, call the Richmond Police Department at 765-983-7247.
cases.summary: Marilyn "Niqui" McCown, 28, of Richmond, Indiana, vanished on July 22, 2001, weeks before her planned August wedding. She had been doing laundry at a Richmond laundromat near South 10th Street; she told her mother men there had been bothering her, then left her mother's house that afternoon and was not seen again. About four months later the GMC Jimmy she had been driving (her fiancé's vehicle, per NBC) was found at The Meadows of Catalpa apartment complex in Dayton, Ohio; the ignition had been tampered with and the stereo was gone, but there were no signs of a struggle, and her folded laundry was in the vehicle. She worked as an accounting clerk at the Montgomery Education and Pre-Release Center in Dayton. Richmond police have never charged anyone. Det. Roger Redmond was the original detective; Det. Mike Wright now leads the case and said in 2026 that evidence, including items from the car, would be re-examined for DNA and fingerprints. Police have publicly described a deceased former co-worker as a person of interest; he was never charged in her case (see theories and flags). Her fiancé, who died in 2021, and her daughter's father were ruled out, per NBC/Western Wayne News.

cases.audioScript: In 1996, investigators searched Fox Hollow Farm, a large estate in Westfield, Indiana, owned by Herb Baumeister, a local businessman. In the woods behind the house they found more than ten thousand human bones and bone fragments. Baumeister had been suspected in the disappearances of several men from Indianapolis. After the search, he fled to Ontario, Canada, where he died by suicide. He was never charged with any of the killings. For decades, most of the men whose remains were found at Fox Hollow had no names. Then, in recent years, the Hamilton County Coroner's Office reopened the work with modern DNA testing. In November 2025, the coroner confirmed by DNA the identity of Roger Goodlet, reported missing from Indianapolis in 1994. The office now counts eleven identified victims. Investigators have also developed a twelfth DNA profile that still belongs to an unknown man, and they are using genetic genealogy to try to give him his name back. If you had a family member who went missing from the Indianapolis area in the 1980s or '90s, the Hamilton County Coroner's Office wants to hear from you.
cases.summary: In 1996 investigators searched Fox Hollow Farm, Herb Baumeister's estate in Westfield, Hamilton County, and recovered more than 10,000 bones and bone fragments. Baumeister had been suspected in the disappearances of several men from Indianapolis in the early 1990s. He fled to Ontario, Canada, where he died by suicide (July 3, 1996, at Pinery Provincial Park per Wikipedia); he was never charged. Since 2022 the Hamilton County Coroner's Office, led by Jeff Jellison, has used advanced forensic and DNA analysis to identify remains. As of its 2025 annual report, 11 victims had been positively identified, and a 12th DNA profile from an unknown individual was undergoing genetic genealogy. In November 2025 the coroner confirmed by DNA that remains belonged to Roger Goodlet (counted as the 11th identified by WISH; WRTV said 10 identified at that point), reported missing from Indianapolis in 1994 and tentatively identified by dental records in 1996. The coroner's investigation remains ongoing.
cases.solvedHow: Never prosecuted: the identified suspect died in 1996 before charges. Ongoing work focuses on identifying victims through forensic anthropology, DNA analysis and investigative genetic genealogy.

cases.audioScript: For more than thirty years, a killer who called himself BTK, for bind, torture, kill, terrorized Wichita, Kansas. It began on January fifteenth, 1974, when he murdered Joseph and Julie Otero and two of their children. Months later he killed twenty-one-year-old Kathryn Bright; her brother was shot but survived. He killed again in 1977, 1985, 1986 and 1991, and he taunted police and the media with letters and riddles. Then he went silent, until 2004, when a new letter arrived at The Wichita Eagle. In early 2005 he sent investigators a computer diskette, and it was traced to his church, where he served as congregation president. On February twenty-fifth, 2005, police arrested Dennis Rader, a Park City civil servant, Scout leader and family man. In June he pleaded guilty to all ten murders. In August 2005 he was sentenced to ten consecutive life terms, a minimum of one hundred seventy-five years. Victims' families told the court the wounds will never heal.
cases.summary: The BTK killer, who named himself for "bind, torture, kill," murdered 10 people in the Wichita, Kansas, area between 1974 and 1991 and taunted police and news media with messages. His first victims were Joseph and Julie Otero and two of their children, killed on Jan. 15, 1974; Kathryn Bright, 21, was killed that April. After years of silence, BTK resurfaced in 2004 with a letter to The Wichita Eagle containing photos of a 1986 victim, and a computer diskette he later sent was traced to his church. Dennis Rader, a Park City resident, church council president and Scout leader, was arrested Feb. 25, 2005, pleaded guilty in June 2005 to 10 murders, and on Aug. 18, 2005 was sentenced by Judge Gregory Waller to 10 consecutive life terms. In 2023, an Oklahoma sheriff's office searched his former Park City property while investigating whether he was tied to other unsolved cases; he has not been charged in any other case.
cases.solvedHow: Solved after BTK's own 2004-05 communications: metadata on a floppy diskette he mailed pointed to his church and to him; he was arrested and confessed, then pleaded guilty.
cases.techniques: Digital forensics (diskette metadata); Analysis of mailed communications; Interrogation/confession; Guilty plea

cases.audioScript: On August twenty-sixth, 1995, twenty-three-year-old Heather Teague was sunbathing on Newburgh Beach, a strip of sand on the Kentucky side of the Ohio River near Spottsville. Across the river in Indiana, a man looking through a telescope saw a shirtless, bearded man come out of the trees around a quarter to one in the afternoon, grab a woman by the hair, and drag her into the woods. He told police he thought the man had a gun. Searchers later found part of Heather's bathing suit near the spot. Kentucky State Police focused on a local man, Marty Dill, whose red Ford Bronco matched a vehicle seen at the beach. Days later, as officers surrounded his trailer, Dill died of what police say was a self-inflicted gunshot. He was never charged, and his family disputes that he was involved. In 2025, state police exhumed his body for DNA testing, but the results have not been released. Heather has never been found. Her mother is still searching, three decades later. If you know where Heather Teague is, call Kentucky State Police Post sixteen in Henderson.
cases.summary: On Aug. 26, 1995, Heather Teague, 23, was sunbathing on Newburgh Beach in Henderson County, Kentucky, when a witness watching from across the Ohio River through a telescope saw a man approach her about 12:45 p.m. and drag her into the woods, apparently at gunpoint. Part of her bathing suit was found near the scene. Kentucky State Police quickly focused on Marvin Ray 'Marty' Dill, whose red-and-white Ford Bronco matched a vehicle reported at the beach; on Sept. 1, 1995, as police and the FBI surrounded his trailer in Poole, Kentucky, he died of what police say was a self-inflicted gunshot wound. He was never charged. Teague's mother and Dill's family have disputed that he matched the abductor's description. KSP exhumed Dill's body on Aug. 25, 2025, to collect DNA; in 2026 KSP denied a records request for the results. Teague has never been found, and KSP says the case remains open.

cases.audioScript: In May 1968, a man collecting old glass insulators near U.S. 25 in Scott County, Kentucky, noticed a tarp lying in a field near the Sadieville exit. Inside, wrapped in canvas like the kind used for tents, was the body of a young woman. She had been killed by a blow to the head. No one could identify her. A newspaper named her "Tent Girl," and in 1971 she was buried in Georgetown under a donated headstone bearing that name. Nearly thirty years later, Todd Matthews, the son-in-law of the man who found her, came across a posting on a missing-persons website. A family was searching for their sister Barbara, missing since late 1967 from the Lexington area. Investigators exhumed Tent Girl's remains, and DNA compared with Barbara's sister was a match. In April 1998, the Scott County Sheriff's Office announced her name: Barbara Ann Hackmann Taylor. She was twenty-four, a young mother living in Lexington. She was finally buried under her own name. But her murder has never been solved, and no one has ever been charged.
cases.summary: In May 1968 Wilbur Riddle, collecting insulators off U.S. 25 near the Sadieville exit in Scott County, found the body of a young woman wrapped in tent canvas and tied with twine, about 13 miles north of Lexington. She had been killed by a blow to the head. Unidentified, she was dubbed "Tent Girl" and buried in Georgetown Cemetery in 1971 under a donated headstone. In 1998 Todd Matthews, who had married Riddle's daughter, matched a missing-person posting by the Hackmann family — for a sister missing since late 1967 from the Lexington area — to the case. Scott County officials exhumed the remains; DNA from her sister matched. In April 1998 the Scott County Sheriff's Office identified her as Barbara Ann "Bobbie" Hackmann Taylor, 24, who had been living in Lexington with her husband and infant. She was reburied under her name in April 1998. The homicide remains unsolved; no one has been charged.
cases.solvedHow: Identification (not the homicide) was solved in 1998: an internet missing-person posting matched by a civilian researcher, followed by exhumation and DNA comparison with a sibling. The homicide remains unsolved.

cases.audioScript: On the night of July third, 2015, thirty-five-year-old Crystal Rogers, a mother of five in Bardstown, Kentucky, was seen for the last time. Two days later, her mother reported her missing. Crystal's car, a red Chevrolet Impala, was found abandoned with a flat tire on the Bluegrass Parkway. Her keys, phone and purse were still inside. For years the case drew national attention, and the FBI canvassed Bardstown, asking residents where they had been in the early morning hours of July fourth. In 2023, prosecutors charged Crystal's boyfriend, Brooks Houck, the father of her youngest son, along with a former employee of his, Joseph Lawson. In 2025, juries convicted Houck of murder, Joseph Lawson of conspiracy to commit murder, and Lawson's father, Steve Lawson, of conspiracy. Houck was sentenced to life in prison, Joseph Lawson to twenty-five years, and Steve Lawson to seventeen years. Appeals have been announced. Crystal's body has never been found. At sentencing, her mother asked the man convicted of killing her daughter one thing: tell us where she is.
cases.summary: Crystal Rogers, 35, a Bardstown mother of five, was last seen the night of July 3, 2015. Her mother reported her missing on July 5. Her red Chevrolet Impala was found abandoned with a flat tire on the Bluegrass Parkway with her keys, phone and purse inside. FBI Louisville spent years searching Bardstown and asking residents where they were in the early hours of July 4, 2015. In September 2023 her boyfriend Brooks Houck (father of her youngest child) and his former employee Joseph Lawson were charged. Joseph's father, Steve Lawson, was tried separately and convicted in May 2025 of conspiracy to commit murder and tampering, receiving 17 years in August 2025. After a trial moved to Warren County, a jury convicted Houck of murder (principal or accomplice) and tampering and Joseph Lawson of conspiracy and tampering on July 7–8, 2025. On Sept. 17, 2025, Nelson Circuit Judge Charles Simms III sentenced Houck to life and Lawson to 25 years. cases.audioScript: On the evening of March twenty-ninth, 2010, thirty-seven-year-old paramedic Annamarie Cochrane Rintala was found dead in the basement of the home she shared with her wife in Granby, a small town in western Massachusetts. She had been strangled. In 2011, a grand jury indicted her wife, Cara Rintala, also a paramedic, on a charge of first-degree murder. What followed became one of the longest legal sagas in Hampshire County history. Two trials, in 2013 and 2014, ended with deadlocked juries. At a third trial in 2016, Cara Rintala was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life without parole. But in 2021, the state's highest court threw out that verdict, ruling that a prosecution witness's testimony about paint found at the scene was unreliable. At a fourth trial in 2023, a jury convicted her of the lesser charge of voluntary manslaughter. She was sentenced to twelve to fourteen years. In July 2026, the Massachusetts Appeals Court upheld that conviction. For Annamarie's family, the district attorney said, it finally brought some closure, sixteen years after she died.
cases.summary: Annamarie Cochrane Rintala, 37, a paramedic, was found strangled in the basement of the Granby, Massachusetts, home she shared with her wife, Cara Rintala, on March 29, 2010. A grand jury indicted Cara Rintala for first-degree murder in 2011. Her first two trials (2013 and 2014) ended in mistrials after juries deadlocked. At a third trial in 2016 she was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life without parole. In 2021 the Supreme Judicial Court vacated that conviction, holding that a paint-industry witness's testimony about when and how paint was poured at the scene was unreliable expert evidence. At a fourth trial in October 2023, a Hampshire Superior Court jury convicted her of voluntary manslaughter; on October 19, 2023, she was sentenced to 12 to 14 years with credit for about seven and a half years served. In July 2026 the Massachusetts Appeals Court affirmed the manslaughter conviction.
cases.solvedHow: Resolved through prosecution of the victim's spouse; after two hung juries and a reversed murder conviction, a fourth jury returned a voluntary manslaughter verdict that was upheld on appeal.
cases.techniques: Grand jury indictment; Time-of-death and scene evidence at trial; Appellate review (SJC 2021; Appeals Court 2026)

cases.audioScript: On a Friday night in June 1996, twenty-year-old Karina Holmer went out with friends to celebrate the summer solstice in Boston. Karina had come from Sweden that spring to work as an au pair, caring for two children in the suburb of Dover. That night she went to the Zanzibar nightclub on Boylston Place, next to Boston Common. She was last seen around 3:20 in the morning near Tremont Street and Boylston Place. On Sunday afternoon, June twenty-third, the upper half of her body was found in a trash bag in a dumpster behind 1091 Boylston Street, in the Fenway. The medical examiner determined she had been strangled. Police interviewed hundreds of people, but neither the crime scene nor the rest of her remains has ever been found. Thirty years later, no one has been charged. Boston police say the case remains open, and they are still asking for help. If you know anything, call the Boston Police Homicide Unit at 617-343-4470, or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-494-TIPS. Karina had planned to go home to Sweden that August.

On the afternoon of June 23 the top half of her dismembered body was found in a trash bag in a dumpster behind 1091 Boylston St. in the Fenway. The medical examiner determined she had been strangled. Police interviewed hundreds of people, but neither a crime scene nor the lower half of her body has been found, and no one has been charged. At the 30th anniversary in June 2026 Boston police renewed their appeal. Persons investigated over the years are not named here because no one has been charged.

cases.audioScript: Just after Christmas in 2010, sixteen-year-old Phylicia Barnes, an honors student from Monroe, North Carolina, was visiting her older half-sister in northwest Baltimore. On December twenty-eighth, she exchanged texts with her sister around midday, and was seen at the apartment in the early afternoon. By evening, she was gone. Her disappearance set off months of intense searches. On April twentieth, 2011, people spotted a body in the Susquehanna River near the Conowingo Dam, about forty miles away. Dental records confirmed it was Phylicia, and the medical examiner ruled her death a homicide. In 2012, police arrested a man and charged him with murder. But over three trials, the case fell apart: a conviction was thrown out, a retrial ended in a mistrial, and in 2018 a judge acquitted him. No one else has been charged, and no one stands convicted of killing Phylicia Barnes. Her family is still waiting for justice. If you know anything about what happened to Phylicia between December twenty-eighth and April of 2011, contact the Baltimore Police Department or Metro Crime Stoppers of Maryland.
cases.summary: Phylicia Simone Barnes, 16, of Monroe, North Carolina, disappeared on Dec. 28, 2010, while visiting her older half-sister at an apartment in northwest Baltimore near Reisterstown Road Plaza. Her body was found on the morning of April 20, 2011, in the Susquehanna River near the Conowingo Dam; she was identified through dental records, and the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner ruled her death a homicide. In April 2012 Baltimore police arrested a man, who was charged with first-degree murder. He was convicted of second-degree murder in February 2013, but the conviction was vacated in 2013 over undisclosed evidence; a 2014 retrial ended in a mistrial; and on March 30, 2018, a Baltimore judge granted a judgment of acquittal in a third trial. No one has been convicted.

cases.audioScript: In January 1999, eighteen-year-old Hae Min Lee, a senior at Woodlawn High School outside Baltimore, disappeared after school. Weeks later, her body was found buried in Baltimore's Leakin Park. Her former boyfriend, Adnan Syed, then seventeen, was charged. In 2000, a jury convicted him of first-degree murder, and he was sentenced to life in prison. Years later, the case became one of the most debated in the country. In September 2022, Baltimore prosecutors moved to vacate his conviction over problems with the evidence. A judge agreed, and Syed walked free after more than twenty years. But Hae's brother appealed, saying the family hadn't been given proper notice of that hearing, and in 2023 the appellate court reinstated the conviction. In March 2025, a judge reduced his sentence to time served under a Maryland law for people convicted as juveniles. Syed remains free, and his murder conviction still stands. Through all of it, Hae Min Lee's family has asked that she be remembered.
cases.summary: Hae Min Lee, 18, a Woodlawn High School student, disappeared Jan. 13, 1999; her body was found in Baltimore's Leakin Park on Feb. 9, 1999 (exact dates per Wikipedia). Her former boyfriend Adnan Syed, then 17, was convicted in February 2000 of first-degree murder, kidnapping, robbery and false imprisonment and sentenced to life plus 30 years. In September 2022, Baltimore prosecutors moved to vacate the conviction over unreliable evidence; a judge granted the motion and Syed was released after nearly 24 years in prison. In March 2023 the Appellate Court of Maryland reinstated the conviction, finding the circuit court violated the rights of Lee's brother, Young Lee, to notice of the hearing; Maryland's Supreme Court held in 2024 (Syed v. Lee, 488 Md. 527) that Young Lee was denied reasonable notice of the vacatur hearing and remanded; the State had entered a nolle prosequi in October 2022 before the reinstatement. On March 6, 2025, Baltimore Circuit Judge Jennifer Schiffer ruled under the Juvenile Restoration Act that Syed should serve no more time, and on March 14, 2025, she formally resentenced him to time served plus five years' supervised probation. His conviction stands.

cases.audioScript: On the evening of October second, 2002, a fifty-five-year-old man was shot dead in a grocery store parking lot in Wheaton, Maryland. By ten the next morning, five more people were dead. One was cutting grass. One was a taxi driver at a gas station. One was vacuuming her van. They were shot at random, from a distance. For three weeks, the shootings terrorized the Washington region. The victims ranged in age from twenty-five to seventy-two. One was an FBI intelligence analyst, killed outside a home improvement store with her husband beside her. Montgomery County Police Chief Charles Moose led the hunt, with the FBI and many other agencies. The break came when a caller linked the shootings to a robbery in Montgomery, Alabama. A fingerprint from that scene matched a teenager named Lee Boyd Malvo. That led to John Allen Muhammad, and to a blue Chevy Caprice. On October twenty-fourth, police found the two asleep in the car at a Maryland rest stop. The rifle was in the trunk. Ten people were killed. Muhammad was executed in Virginia in 2009. Malvo was sentenced to life in prison.
cases.summary: Between Oct. 2 and Oct. 22, 2002, snipers killed 10 people and critically wounded three in Maryland, Virginia and Washington, D.C. (FBI). The first victim, James D. Martin, 55, was killed in a Wheaton, Md., grocery store parking lot on Oct. 2; five more were killed in Montgomery County and Washington the next day (AP via CBS). The Montgomery County Police Department, led by Chief Charles Moose, ran the investigation with the FBI, ATF and other agencies. A caller claiming to be the sniper linked the shootings to a robbery in Montgomery, Alabama; a fingerprint on a magazine from that scene matched Lee Boyd Malvo, which led investigators to John Allen Muhammad and a 1990 Chevrolet Caprice registered in New Jersey (FBI). Early on Oct. 24, 2002, Maryland State Police, Montgomery County SWAT and the FBI Hostage Rescue Team arrested both men asleep in the car at a rest stop off I-70 in Maryland; a Bushmaster .223 rifle was in the trunk (FBI). The Justice Department sent Muhammad to Prince William County, Va., for capital murder prosecution (DOJ). He was executed by lethal injection at Greensville Correctional Center on Nov. 10, 2009, for the killing of Dean Harold Meyers; Malvo was sentenced to life in prison (AP via Spokesman-Review; NBC4; ABC News).
cases.solvedHow: A caller claiming to be the sniper linked the spree to an Alabama robbery-murder; fingerprint evidence there identified Malvo, leading to Muhammad and the car, which was spotted at a Maryland rest stop.

cases.audioScript: Shortly after midnight on May fourteenth, 2008, nineteen-year-old Brandon Swanson was driving home to Marshall, Minnesota, after celebrating the end of the semester with friends in Canby. His car slid into a ditch on a gravel road. He wasn't hurt. He called his parents, who drove out to find him while staying on the phone with him. Brandon thought he was near the small town of Lynd and started walking toward lights. Then Brandon shouted an expletive, and the line went silent. His parents called back again and again. No answer. Cell phone records later showed he wasn't near Lynd at all. His car was found about twenty miles away, near Taunton. Search dogs tracked his scent for miles, toward the Yellow Medicine River, and lost it there. Years of searches, including digs in the riverbed, have found nothing. His parents' fight led to Brandon's Law, which requires police in Minnesota to act quickly on missing adults. Brandon is still missing. If you know anything, call the Minnesota BCA at 651-793-7000.
cases.summary: In the early hours of May 14, 2008, Brandon Swanson, 19, was driving home to Marshall from Canby when his car went into a ditch. He called his parents at about 12:30 a.m.; they drove out to help but could not find him. He said he would walk toward the lights of Lynd and stayed on the phone; he swore and the call ended abruptly (BCA; Forum News Service). The Charley Project puts the end of the call shortly after 2:00 a.m.; Solve the Case says it went silent 47 minutes into the call. Using cell phone records, authorities found his car later that day off a gravel road near Taunton, about 20 miles from where he believed he was (BCA bulletin; Forum News Service; Charley Project). Search dogs tracked a scent about three miles to the Yellow Medicine River and lost it there. Searches of the river, including a 2021 excavation during drought, found nothing (Forum News Service). His parents lobbied for Brandon's Law (2009), which requires prompt investigation of missing adults (MPR News). Investigators continue to receive tips; Brandon has never been found.

cases.audioScript: On December sixteenth, 2004, twenty-three-year-old Bobbie Jo Stinnett was at home here in Skidmore, a town of about three hundred people. She was eight months pregnant. She bred rat terriers, and a woman had arranged to come see her puppies. That woman was Lisa Montgomery, who had driven from Melvern, Kansas, using a fake name. Montgomery strangled Bobbie Jo, cut the baby from her body, and drove away with the newborn. Bobbie Jo's mother found her that afternoon. Computer investigators traced the online messages to Montgomery's home, more than one hundred thirty miles away. The next day, police found her with the baby girl. The baby was alive, and she was returned to her father. Montgomery confessed. A federal jury convicted her of kidnapping resulting in death and recommended a death sentence. On January thirteenth, 2021, she became the first woman executed by the federal government in nearly seven decades. The crime shocked Skidmore. The county sheriff said nobody there could ever have imagined it.
cases.summary: Bobbie Jo Stinnett, 23, ran a rat terrier breeding business from her home in Skidmore, Missouri, and was eight months pregnant in December 2004. Lisa Montgomery, who lived in Melvern, Kansas, and had falsely claimed to be pregnant, contacted Stinnett on Dec. 15, 2004, under the alias Darlene Fischer about buying a puppy. On Dec. 16, Montgomery arrived at Stinnett's home around 12:30 p.m., strangled her, cut into her abdomen and removed the baby, and drove away with the infant. Stinnett's mother found her later that afternoon. Computer investigators traced the alias e-mail to Montgomery's home more than 130 miles away, and on Dec. 17 authorities found her with a newborn girl; she confessed to strangling Stinnett and taking the baby. The baby survived and was returned to her father. A federal jury convicted Montgomery of kidnapping resulting in death and recommended death; the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit affirmed on April 5, 2011. Montgomery was executed at the U.S. Penitentiary in Terre Haute, Indiana, on Jan. 13, 2021, the first woman executed by the federal government in nearly seven decades.
cases.solvedHow: Solved within a day: computer investigators traced the alias online messages to Montgomery's Kansas home, where surveillance found her with the newborn; she confessed.

cases.audioScript: Just before midnight on Friday, June fifteenth, 2018, security cameras in downtown Missoula, Montana, recorded twenty-three-year-old Jermain Charlo socializing outside a bar called The Badlander. Jermain was a mother of two and a member of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes. Shortly before midnight she walked away down the alley with a man she knew, and in the early morning hours of June sixteenth, she disappeared. She stopped posting on social media and stopped checking in with her grandmother, and her family knew something was wrong. On June twentieth, her aunt drove to Missoula to file a missing-person report in person. Missoula Police Detective Guy Baker led the investigation and said he had no doubt she was the victim of a criminal act. Searches came up empty, and police later released never-before-seen security video to CBS's 48 Hours, hoping someone would remember something. No one has been arrested, and police have not publicly named a suspect. If you were in downtown Missoula that night, or you know anything about what happened to Jermain, contact the Missoula Police Department.
cases.summary: Jermain Charlo, 23, a mother of two and a member of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes, disappeared in Missoula, Montana, in the early morning hours of June 16, 2018. Security video released by Missoula police shows her walking downtown and socializing outside The Badlander bar shortly before midnight on June 15, then leaving the area with a man she knew. In a June 21, 2018 appeal, Missoula police said she was last seen near Orange and South Fifth streets, wearing jeans, a white T-shirt, a brown Under Armour sweater and cowboy boots. The man first said he dropped her off at the Orange Street Food Farm, then told police it was a residential area about eight blocks west of the store; he has never been named a suspect and is not named here (CBS News). Her aunt filed a missing-person report in person with Missoula police on June 20, 2018. Lead detective Guy Baker said in 2020 that he had no doubt she was the victim of a criminal act, and NBC Montana reported an $11,000 reward at that time. Baker retired from the department in 2025 after taking part in dozens of searches for her. No one has been arrested and no suspects have been publicly named.

cases.audioScript: Just before Christmas in 1996, twelve-year-old Celina Mays went to bed at a family home on Crestview Drive in Willingboro, New Jersey, at about eleven at night. She was nine months pregnant, with her baby due around December twenty-ninth. The next morning, her bed held only pillows arranged under the blankets. Her purse and her prenatal vitamins were left behind. Celina has not been heard from since. Police say they have run down more than two hundred and fifty leads over the years. Investigators have said the family had close ties to a small church in nearby Mount Holly, the Gospel of Christ Ministries, which is now an abandoned building, and they are still looking for people who attended or worked there. The father of Celina's baby has never been identified. Willingboro police and the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children say they remain hopeful that Celina, and her child, may still be alive, perhaps living under another name. Today Celina would be in her forties. If you know anything about Celina Janette Mays, or about that church in the mid-1990s, call the Willingboro Township Police Department.
cases.summary: Celina Janette Mays, 12, of Willingboro, New Jersey, was nine months pregnant when she disappeared during the night of Dec. 15-16, 1996. Per the Charley Project and Solve the Case listings, she went to bed about 11 p.m. at her aunt's residence on Crestview Drive, where she lived with her father and other relatives; the next morning pillows were found under her blankets, and her prenatal vitamins, purse and other belongings had been left behind. CBS Philadelphia (2022) reported that Willingboro police had investigated more than 254 leads and that the family was closely tied to the Gospel of Christ Ministry church in Mount Holly, whose pastor (Celina's aunt) has since died. NCMEC (2024) reported that police have not identified the father of Celina's child and that the church building is now abandoned. Police have said she could be living under a different name. No one has been charged, and the case remains an open missing-person investigation.

cases.audioScript: On February second, 2009, a woman walking her dog on Albuquerque's West Mesa noticed a bone sticking out of the dirt along the trail. It was human. Over the following weeks, detectives uncovered the skeletal remains of eleven women and one unborn child, buried in makeshift graves near 118th Street Southwest. Investigators have now identified all eleven victims. One of them, Jamie Barela, was fifteen years old. The others were Monica Candelaria, Victoria Chavez, Virginia Cloven, Syllannia Edwards, Cinnamon Elks, Doreen Marquez, Julie Nieto, Veronica Romero, Evelyn Salazar, and Michelle Valdez. Police say the case remains active and open. More than fifteen hundred tips have come in over the years, and every one has been followed up. No one has ever been charged. The Albuquerque Police Department is offering a reward of one hundred thousand dollars for information leading to an arrest and conviction. If you know anything, call the West Mesa task force at 505-768-2450, or Crime Stoppers at 505-843-STOP. These were daughters, sisters and mothers, and their families are still waiting.
cases.summary: On Feb. 2, 2009, a woman walking her dog on Albuquerque's west side found a bone protruding from an earthen trail. Over the following weeks detectives uncovered the skeletal remains of 11 women and one unborn child buried in makeshift graves near 118th Street SW on the West Mesa. All 11 victims have been identified: Jamie Barela (15), Monica Candelaria, Victoria Chavez, Virginia Cloven, Syllannia Edwards, Cinnamon Elks, Doreen Marquez, Julie Nieto, Veronica Romero, Evelyn Salazar and Michelle Valdez. APD says ten of the victims shared a common link; Jamie Barela had no known involvement in it. No one has been charged. In 2026 APD said the case remains an active and open investigation with persons of interest still being investigated, more than 1,500 tips received, and a $100,000 reward for information leading to an arrest and conviction.

cases.audioScript: At nine-thirty on the morning of September twentieth, 1988, nineteen-year-old Tara Calico left her home in Belen, New Mexico, for a bike ride, riding her mother's bicycle because her own was damaged. She rode the same thirty-six-mile route every day. At about eleven forty-five, she was last seen riding along Highway 47 in Valencia County, and she was never seen again. The only evidence found was a Boston cassette tape and a piece of her Walkman. For more than three decades, local, state and federal investigators worked the case. In June 2023, Valencia County Sheriff Denise Vigil said there was enough evidence to send the case to the district attorney for review of potential charges. The identities of the persons of interest are sealed by the court. As of September 2025, no charges had been filed, and the sheriff's office was setting insect traps in an abandoned mine shaft north of Belen in the search for her remains. Tara's parents have died, but her sisters and brothers are still waiting for answers. The FBI offers a reward of up to twenty thousand dollars. If you know anything, contact the Valencia County Sheriff's Office or the FBI's Albuquerque field office at tips dot F B I dot gov.
cases.summary: Tara Leigh Calico, 19, left her home in Belen, New Mexico, at 9:30 a.m. on Sept. 20, 1988, for a bike ride on her mother's bicycle, as her own was damaged. She was last seen riding along Highway 47 in Valencia County at about 11:45 a.m. on her routine 36-mile route and was never seen again. The only evidence found on a dirt road was a Boston cassette tape and a piece of her Walkman cassette player. She was a sophomore at the University of New Mexico-Valencia campus studying psychology; her mother, Patty Doel, died in May 2006. On June 13, 2023, Valencia County Sheriff Denise Vigil said the investigation was complete and there was sufficient evidence to submit it to the district attorney's office for review of potential charges; the identities of persons of interest are sealed by the court. In September 2025 the Albuquerque Journal reported that no charges had been filed and the DA had not declined the case, that the results of a 2021 search of a Valencia County residence (April per the Journal; fall per the News-Bulletin) were sealed by a district judge, and that Lt. Joseph Rowland was using insect traps in an abandoned mine shaft north of Belen. The FBI offers a reward of up to $20,000. A 1989 Polaroid found in Port St. Joe, Florida, was one of the most-publicized tips in the case; it has never been confirmed to show Calico.

cases.audioScript: In 1979, nineteen-year-old Gwenn Marie Story left the Cincinnati area with two male friends, hoping to find her biological father in California. Her family never heard from her again. On August fourteenth, 1979, a man walking through an open field near Sahara Avenue and Las Vegas Boulevard, where the El Rancho Vegas once stood, found the body of a young woman. The coroner ruled her death a homicide, and no one could identify her, so detectives called her Sahara Sue Doe. In the fall of 2022, Las Vegas police cold case detectives asked for forensic genetic genealogy, and the Texas lab Othram took on the case. On November fifteenth, 2023, forty-four years later, Othram told police she had been identified as Gwenn Marie Story. Her family says they were told the men left her in Las Vegas. Her name is known now, but her killer is not. Metro's Cold Case Section is still investigating, and asks anyone with information about Gwenn or the men she traveled with to call Crime Stoppers at 702-385-5555.
cases.summary: Gwenn Marie Story, 19, left the Cincinnati area in 1979 with two male friends to look for her biological father in California, and her family never heard from her again. On Aug. 14, 1979, a man walking through a field on the former El Rancho Vegas site, in the area of Sahara Avenue and Las Vegas Boulevard, found her body; the Clark County coroner ruled the death a homicide. News 3 reports investigators said she was stabbed to death. Unidentified, she became known as "Sahara Sue Doe." In fall 2022 LVMPD's cold case detectives requested forensic genetic genealogy and sent her remains to Othram in Texas, and on Nov. 15, 2023, Othram notified police she had been identified. LVMPD homicide Lt. Jason Johansson confirmed the identification and said the homicide remains unsolved. Her family told investigators they were told the men she traveled with left her in Las Vegas; the men are not named here. In May 2026, News 3 reported the search for her killer continues, with the Vegas Justice League supporting LVMPD's genealogy work.

cases.audioScript: On Thanksgiving night, November twenty-second, 1984, fourteen-year-old Wendy Jerome of Rochester, New York, left home to deliver a birthday card to a friend nearby. She never came home. When she missed her curfew, her mother, Marlene, called Wendy's friends and then the police. That night, Rochester police found Wendy's body on Webster Avenue near School Number Thirty-Three. She had been raped and murdered. Police preserved the scene, and for decades the case stayed open. As DNA technology improved, analysts tested Wendy's clothing and other evidence. Investigators turned to familial DNA testing, and in 2020, nearly thirty-six years later, they arrested Timothy Williams, who had lived in Wendy's neighborhood and was twenty at the time. His first trial ended in a mistrial. At a retrial in March 2024, a jury convicted him of three counts of second-degree murder, the first conviction in New York State built on familial DNA. In April 2024 he was sentenced to twenty-five years to life. Her mother said Wendy was the sweetest, most caring little girl in the whole world.
cases.summary: On Thanksgiving night, Nov. 22, 1984, Wendy Jerome, 14, went to deliver a birthday card to a nearby friend in Rochester and did not return. Her mother called friends and then police, and Rochester police found her body that night on Webster Avenue near School No. 33; she had been raped and murdered (Monroe County DA). The case went cold. As DNA methods improved, evidence including her clothing was tested, and familial DNA testing led investigators to Timothy Williams, who lived in the neighborhood and was 20 in 1984 (13WHAM). He was arrested in 2020. A first trial in late 2023 ended in a mistrial over alleged juror misconduct. On March 8, 2024, a jury convicted him of three counts of second-degree murder, which the DA called the first conviction using familial DNA in New York State. On April 17, 2024, Justice Alex Renzi sentenced him to three concurrent terms of 25 years to life. His defense said it would appeal; no appellate decision was found.
